title: R3 Lithium launches lithium recycling facility in Georgia - electrive.com
content:
R3 Lithium has started producing lithium carbonate from recycled battery materials in the US state of Georgia. The existing plant is designed for 2,500 tons per year and is now being transitioned to continuous commercial operation.
The plant in Covington is designed to produce 2,500 tons of lithium carbonate annually.
Image: R3 Lithium
R3 Lithium took over the approximately 14,300 square metre facility in Covington only in July 2026. The previous owner –
the insolvent company Ascend Elements
– had, according to the company, invested around $150 million in the site. As early as 2025, lithium carbonate with a purity of 99 per cent was produced there entirely from recycled feedstock. R3 therefore describes Covington as the first commercially proven facility of its kind in North America.
The site combines several recycling stages. The shredding plants have an annual capacity of 30,000 tonnes and process production scrap and end-of-life batteries into black mass. From this, R3 recovers the lithium on-site using a calcination-based crystallisation and water-based precipitation process. The remaining concentrate of nickel, cobalt, manganese and graphite is to be marketed separately.
The existing line can produce 2,500 tonnes of lithium carbonate annually. Space for a second line of the same size is already planned, but R3 has not specified a timeline for the possible doubling. Initially, $15 million dollars from a Series A financing round will be invested in upgrading the facility for continuous commercial operation.
R3 to expand lithium carbonate production
On the sales side, R3 points to signed offtake agreements worth around one billion dollars, including with the commodity trader Trafigura. However, the company does not disclose quantities, durations or prices, making it difficult to assess the contract value.
While Smackover Lithium aims to extract new lithium from brine, R3 focuses on existing material from the battery supply chain. The challenge now lies in continuous operation. Black mass can vary significantly depending on cell chemistry, age and origin of the batteries. R3 must therefore demonstrate that different input materials can be reliably processed into lithium carbonate with the specified purity.
In the long term, R3 plans additional facilities in North America and Europe. For the Covington site, however, the focus is initially on ramping up production. It has already been demonstrated that lithium carbonate can be produced from
recycled material
. Whether the process can also function continuously and economically on a commercial scale remains to be seen. R3 has not yet provided details on yield or production costs.

title: Beyond the QR code: Why battery passports are just the beginning – Batteries International
content: The battery industry has spent months debating compliance deadlines, QR codes and data requirements. But according to Ken Davies, CCO at DigiProd Pass, those conversations are missing the bigger picture. Battery passports are not simply another piece of EU regulation. They are the first visible step in a digital revolution that will eventually reshape every manufactured product on the planet . If you think battery passports are simply another layer of European bureaucracy, Ken Davies believes you’re looking through the wrong end of the telescope. Yes, companies selling batteries above 2kWh into the EU will soon have to comply with incoming battery regulation. Yes, every qualifying battery will require a digital passport. And yes, manufacturers across the industry are racing to understand exactly what information those passports will need to contain. But Davies argues that focusing solely on batteries misses the significance of what is happening. “You’ve got to see the battery passport as just one element of a much bigger revolution,” he explains. “Consumer electronics, furniture, textiles, construction materials and countless other industries are all heading in the same direction. Batteries simply happen to be first. The plan within the EU is that all of these sectors will eventually have operational digital product passports.” Credit: DigiProd Pass A revolution driven by data Much of the conversation surrounding battery passports has centred on regulation. Davies believes the real story is consumer empowerment. At its heart, the digital product passport (DPP) is designed to provide transparent information throughout a product’s lifetime, enabling consumers to make better-informed purchasing decisions while giving recyclers and second-life operators the information they need to recover valuable materials efficiently. For years, sustainability has often been discussed in principle rather than practice. According to Davies, legislators are now beginning to create the legal framework that makes genuinely circular supply chains possible. “It’s really a mechanism to empower consumers with data so they can make better informed decisions about what they buy,” he explains. “It also provides organisations involved in recycling and second life with all the data they need to make those activities commercially viable.” The regulation may be arriving through Brussels, but Davies sees it as part of a worldwide movement rather than a uniquely European initiative. China is already developing similar systems, while other markets are expected to introduce their own versions. Although individual regulations may differ, Davies believes the underlying structure will remain remarkably similar. “ If you want to sell something in the EU, you’ll comply with the EU system. If you want to sell in another market, you’ll comply with theirs. Ninety-five per cent of what companies need to do will be exactly the same.” The critical date remains 18 February 2027, when battery passports become mandatory for batteries over 2kWh placed on the EU market. Yet Davies cautions against assuming that reaching the deadline marks the end of the journey. Ken Davies at the 2026 Battery Passport Conference in Lille One of the biggest misconceptions, he argues, is that companies only need to achieve compliance once. “It might be that the passport starts off relatively basic,” he says. “Perhaps it’s simply a QR code with core information. But it won’t stay basic.” Instead, battery passports will evolve continuously as regulators demand increasingly detailed information. “People mustn’t think they’ll reach 18 February, breathe a sigh of relief and forget about it,” he says. “The expectations of the quality of the data will keep expanding.” That evolving nature explains why many companies remain uncertain. The deadline itself is fixed, but some details surrounding the precise content of the passport continue to develop. Who, for instance, will actually be responsible? Many assume it will be the battery manufacturer, but Davies is keen to clarify that this won’t, necessarily, be the case. “Responsibility will fall upon what the regulation defines as the economic operator, which is the company placing the finished product on the market,” he explains. “If you’re Audi, you’re the economic operator.” That means vehicle, truck and drone manufacturers, and countless other OEMs become responsible for ensuring compliant battery passports accompany the products they sell. And this is a distinction that matters. But the regulation is not designed to hold OEMs responsible for every action that occurs throughout global mining supply chains. Rather, it requires transparency. “It doesn’t make Audi responsible for child labour in the Congo,” Davies explains. “It makes them responsible for making sure everybody can see where everything came from.” The emphasis shifts from assigning blame to providing visibility. The real challenge isn’t the QR code When battery passports first emerged, much of the discussion focused on the visible element: the QR code attached to each battery. Davies believes that focus is misplaced. “The QR code isn’t the challenge,” he says. “We could design that in five minutes. Instead, the real work happens behind the scenes. Information has to be collected from multiple business systems that often cannot communicate with one another. Manufacturing records, material data, sourcing information, carbon footprints, repair histories and operational updates all need to be integrated into a single digital record. The real challenge is coordinating the data from different systems and making sure they all work together.” That becomes even more complicated because the passport is not static. Unlike a paper certificate, the battery passport is expected to evolve throughout the battery’s operational life. “If a vehicle is involved in an accident and the battery is affected, the passport has to know that.” Rather than creating a single document, companies are effectively building a living digital record that follows each battery from manufacture through use, second life and ultimately recycling. Batteries may actually have it easier Ironically, despite being first to adopt DPPs, Davies believes the battery industry may ultimately prove one of the easier sectors to implement them as modern battery manufacturing already generates vast quantities of production data. “Gigafactories routinely capture detailed manufacturing information throughout production, making much of the required data readily available. The battery industry is actually very sophisticated in its data management already,” Davies says. “Compare that with textiles. Supply chains often stretch across multiple countries, involving thousands of smaller suppliers with inconsistent digital systems and limited traceability. If you’re making a T-shirt in Bangladesh, that’s a completely different challenge.” The principles remain identical, but the quality and accessibility of the underlying data are vastly different. Worker monitoring textile machines in a factory. SMEs face the biggest hurdle But while large automotive manufacturers already possess sophisticated enterprise resource planning (ERP) and manufacturing systems capable of supporting DPPs, smaller companies face a steeper climb. Many could be forgiven for thinking a simple, low-cost solution exists, but Davies warns against knee-jerking to this assumption. He compares DPP systems with enterprise software. Small companies rarely build their own ERP or CRM platforms from scratch. Instead, they rely on specialist providers. “DPPs will most likely follow the same model,” Davies says. “There isn’t really going to be an easy route.” So as the compliance deadline approaches, many SMEs are going to discover that implementation is neither quick nor inexpensive, yet remains unavoidable if they wish to continue selling qualifying products within Europe. And despite almost all the uncertainties ahead, one striking theme remains. Battery passports will pave the way for an entirely new professional ecosystem, one in which data specialists, systems integrators, compliance experts, software providers and consultants are all likely to play increasingly important roles. “It’s all about the data,” Davies says. “AI will undoubtedly become part of the picture, but effective data management will remain the foundation upon which future compliance is built.” For today’s engineering graduates, entirely new careers may emerge around DPP infrastructure and lifecycle data management and the growing demand for knowledge was something that became evident during the inaugural Battery Passport Conference in Lille earlier this year. Davies says delegates were eager not only to hear presentations but also to compare experiences with one another. “It was difficult getting people back into the conference room after coffee,” he jokes. “Everybody just wanted to keep comparing notes and talking.” For Davies, that was perhaps the clearest indication that the industry recognises both the scale of the challenge and the value of collaboration. Rather than competing over compliance, companies were openly discussing best practice, concerns and practical solutions. “It was an amazing networking experience,” he says. “Delegates really appreciated the opportunity to talk about this subject in isolation and in depth.” Beyond batteries Davies admits he only fully appreciated the scale of the DPP movement around 18 months ago while interviewing experts for his Battery Technology Podcast. Today, he spends his time working across batteries, textiles, construction and other manufacturing sectors – a cross-industry perspective that reinforces the central message that this isn’t just about batteries. It’s everything. For battery manufacturers, this may be the most important takeaway of all. The passport is not simply another compliance box to tick before February 2027. It is the first glimpse of a future in which every significant manufactured product carries a living digital identity, one that documents where it came from, what it contains, how it has been used and ultimately how it should be reused or recycled. For companies still debating whether battery passports are really happening, Davies has one simple analogy. “The train has already left the station,” he says. “The sooner you get on it, the better.” The post Beyond the QR code: Why battery passports are just the beginning appeared first on Batteries International .

title: Why nShift Won Supply Chain Company of the Year
content:
Why nShift Won Supply Chain Company of the Year
Prioritise Us
on Google
The Global Supply Chain Awards 2026
Supply Chain Digital takes a look at the 2026 winner of the Company of the Year Award, acknowledging the leader transforming last-mile delivery
In an era defined by constantly shifting trade relations and legislation, logistics companies have been working hard to
ensure resilience
throughout.
At the Global Supply Chain Awards 2026, one company was recognised for exactly that.
Company of the Year Award
2026 went to nShift – a company which has quietly risen to the top in the global supply chain.
The winners of the Global Supply Chain Awards were announced
Company of the Year
This award was an opportunity to recognise small to mid-sized organisations with less than 1,000 employees. These companies have demonstrated significant agility,
innovation
and performance in their supply chain operations, and the award recognises those who are driving measurable growth in today's competitive market.
Judges looked for outstanding initiatives, a demonstration of adaptability, evidence of innovation and how the company embodies strong leadership.
The other nominees were:
SAAMI TRADESTAR LOGISTICS LIMITED
Seqwater (Silver)
Worldly Holdings Inc. (Bronze)
nShift takes the top spot
won gold
for its behind-the-scenes work in ensuring parcels get delivered on time. Throughout its time, the platform has helped turn last-mile delivery from a source of lost margin into a powerful competitive advantage.
The company has evolved from carrier connectivity, into a platform for multi-carrier shipping and delivery experience. Now, more than 20,000 businesses use nShift to manage their delivery journeys, across more than 190 countries and territories.
nShift is constantly working to grow its operations, having recently
invested in AI
- applying it across delivery assistance, delivery predictions and billing discrepancies.
Jurgen Leijdekker, CEO of nShift
A word on its recognition
Though nShift could not attend the awards, the company has released a response in recognition of its win.
CEO Jurgen Leijdekker wrote: “Winning Company of the Year is powerful recognition of what nShift has become and where we are going.
"For nearly three decades, we have built the critical carrier connectivity that global delivery operations depend on. Now we are adding powerful intelligence and
AI-native
capabilities across that foundation, helping businesses make better decisions, protect delivery economics and create stronger customer experiences.
"This award belongs to the thousands of customers around the world who trust nShift with their delivery journeys every day.”

title: What is Defining the Future of AI in Supply Chains?
content:
What is Defining the Future of AI in Supply Chains?
Prioritise Us
on Google
Leaders offered insights on AI in the supply chain at Supply Chain LIVE
Industry leaders from Baringa, Amazon and Infosys took to the stage at Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit to discuss the future of AI in supply chain
Supply chain executives at Supply Chain LIVE in London explored how to extract real value from AI beyond theoretical promise.
Sameer Mohammed, Partner and Supply Chain Practice Lead at Baringa, Umesh Rangasamy, Leader of Private Brands Supply Chain Technology at Amazon, and Ambeshwar Nath, Executive Vice President and Industry Head of Consumer Goods, Retail and Logistics at Infosys, examined where human oversight remains necessary despite automation advances.
The discussion centred on bridging the gap between AI potential and current operational realities in supply chain management.
Sameer Mohammed, Partner, Supply Chain Practice Lead at Baringa
Value beyond theoretical promise
Practical AI application in supply chain operations differs from theoretical discussions of autonomous systems. Current deployments
provide value
through the system of intelligence layer, which processes disparate near-real-time data to inform decisions.
According to Sameer, expectations around fully autonomous operations exceed current capabilities. "Where I think the hype is maybe too much at this moment in time, is this idea of lights-out and the idea that you can basically run the entire thing without human beings, or at least with a human in the loop to make sure that the AI is effectively doing the right things," he says.
Three barriers prevent full
automation in supply chain
operations. Legal frameworks require human accountability for decisions, the technology still needs context for accurate application, and data quality in many organisations remains insufficient.
Umesh described ongoing experimentation at Amazon in autonomous supply chain responses. "We keep talking about autonomous supply chain where it's just reacting to situations. Supply chain is one of those challenging and also interesting areas where AI can work and make a big difference because things keep changing on a daily basis. So, we're looking at where AI can react to that fast" he says.
Umesh Rangasamy, Leader of Private Brands Supply Chain Technology at Amazon
Operational changes in planning
According to Ambeshwar, AI
implementation at Infosys
reduced client supply chain planner requirements by 30% to 40%. The technology could shift planner workload allocation from 70% reporting and 30% execution to the reverse ratio.
Amazon achieves demand prediction accuracy between 80% and 90% across its retail network, according to Umesh. This accuracy range reflects current capabilities in large-scale supply chain forecasting.
AI-first engineering has changed software development timelines in supply chain systems. Legacy system updates now require less time and lower costs, according to Umesh.
However, complete elimination of human oversight in supply chain operations remains impractical. "It's only when you trust the intelligence and say, 'Look, take action independently.' That's where system engagement comes in," Ambeshwar notes.
Implementation and scaling challenges
Enterprise organisations often attempt to scale pilot programmes without addressing underlying friction in supply chain operations. The panel identified this approach as a common failure point.
Successful AI integration
requires focus on business outcomes rather than technology strategies. Strong data foundations, cross-departmental alignment and executive sponsorship support effective deployment in supply chain environments.
"The question has moved now from, 'What is my AI strategy? What is my AI supposed to do?' to, 'This is the business outcome I want. How can AI help me realise those goals?' The token economics are becoming clear, the cost efficiencies don't seem as apparent once the technology scales up. So, all those parameters are having clients really look at where can you apply it, and do one thing, but do it deep," Ambeshwar says.
Umesh agrees that defining specific business outcomes prevents unfocused AI deployment. "Identifying the business outcome or KPI is key because then that will bring focus," he says. "Otherwise, what happens is AI is going to go all over the place. It's going to try to come up with its own metric."
Ambeshwar Nath, Executive Vice President & Industry Head of Consumer Goods, Retail & Logistics at Infosys
Training and deployment expectations
Out of 330,000 employees at Infosys, 250,000 have received formal AI training, according to Ambeshwar. This training programme could show the scale of workforce preparation required for AI integration in supply chain operations.
According to Umesh, AI models bring solutions to 80% completion quickly, but the final 20% requires substantial human effort. This pattern applies across supply chain technology deployments.
New AI systems in supply chain operations should launch with initial accuracy rates between 80% and 85%, according to Ambeshwar. Expecting immediate perfection creates unrealistic deployment parameters.
Strategic workforce planning for
AI integration
requires organisations to look five to ten years ahead, according to Sameer. This timeline addresses upcoming skill gaps in supply chain management.
Evolving professional roles
AI automation of routine reporting and data aggregation changes supply chain professional responsibilities. The shift moves workers from task execution to strategic oversight functions.
Human roles in AI-enabled supply chain operations focus on relationship building and cross-functional collaboration. Capacity freed by automation allows for strategic problem solving rather than eliminating positions.
The panel indicated that supply chain professionals need
different skills
as AI handles data processing tasks. Long-term planning and contextual decision making remain human responsibilities in automated environments.

title: From Visibility to Resilience: The Kongsberg Maritime Story
content:
Prioritise Us
on Google
Rob Anthony Senior Vice President - Business Support & UK Country Manager, Kongsberg Maritime
Partnerships are more crucial than ever when it comes to driving resilience and visibility in the supply chain, as Ron Anthony from Kongsberg details
Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit included a range of critical conversations, including a keynote hosted by Rob Anthony, SVP – Business Support & UK Country Manager, Kongsberg Maritime.
In his presentation,
in association with IntegrityNext - Rob explored how he and his team approach responsible procurement and use ESG data into actionable insights.
Throughout the event, sustainability, visibility and risk management were all core topics of conversation, demonstrating where supply chain priorities are currently lying.
Steve Cobley, Head of Sales Northern Europe at IntegrityNext
A strong partnership
The panel kicked off with an opening comment by Steve Cobley, Head of Sales Northern Europe at IntegrityNext, who introduced Rob and his keynote. In his speech, Steve talked about how IntegrityNext is working with its partners to
drive visibility
and increase resilience throughout the supply chain.
IntegrityNext has approximately 600 customers using its platform, working across various legislative and
regulatory requirements
. The platform aims to remove the friction from this workflow, operating to drive sustainability and supply chain due diligence.
IntegrityNext, Steve says, can unlock insights into "forced labour, supply chain visibility, carbon and product compliance". Kongsberg Maritime is being supported by the platform as it works to build up its supply chain.
The companies have been working together since 2021, in order to boost Kongsberg's sustainability work and ESG targets with its suppliers.
Kongsberg is a Norwegian maritime business, one of the top organisations in its country, with global capabilities.
"We are a technology partner," explained Rob when he came on stage. "We deliver integrated maritime solutions across the vessel life cycle. We sell to ship owners, we sell to shipyards, we work globally and our supply chains are quite complex, very project based."
A complex supply chain
As a company, Kongsberg's reach is significant, having more than 8,000 employees, more than 8,000 suppliers and supporting more than 30,000 vessels around the world. It aids with thrusters, propulsion, manoeuvring and on-deck equipment.
"So we have all these requirements coming in some of them are legal obligations," Rob explained. "In Norway, we have the Norwegian Transparency Act, and the human rights legislation is the most advanced in the world – even a higher level than the Modern Slavery Act. This requires us to do sub-supplier and supplier checks on human rights."
As a maritime company, Kongsberg also deals with a lot of material regulations from ship recycling, as well as differing legislation on minerals and other products. With this, there is lots of complexity that the company is dealing with in order to meet regulations and help its customers
meet those standards
IntegrityNext
to be able to do self-assessment with suppliers and based on that risk assessment, we'll decide which ones we go and audit."
Rob also explains that some of Kongsberg's customers are using IntegrityNext, which he says is good for creating cohesion across the value chain and reducing admin.
Rob Anthony Senior Vice President - Business Support & UK Country Manager at Kongsberg Maritime
Core areas of focus
IntegrityNext and Kongsberg work together across various focus points in order to improve responsible operations:
Emissions reduction – working together on developing the corporate carbon footprint module to reduce greenhouse gas emissions
Cybersecurity – including audits and exploring risks from supplier questionnaires
Sub-supplier transparency – to improve risk management, tracing where materials come from. This will improve both ESG and compliance, as well as risk management
Digital – integrating AI to add value throughout the company
"In your category strategies, in your sourcing strategies, risk management is probably much higher up the priority list than it was 10 years ago," Rob said. "There's so many risks – geopolitical, critical raw materials, economic – and as a category manager, you need to be really
adaptable and flexible
In today's world of increased risk and complexity, simplicity is the key. IntegrityNext, Rob explains, helps to keep Kongsberg's system simple, helping the company manage its risk and gain extra layers of transparency throughout operations.

title: Tesla reveals European Semi specs: 550 km range, 800 kW charging
content:
Tesla revealed the European specs for its Semi electric truck, and they don’t match the version already in production in the US. The truck will offer up to 550 km (342 miles) of range at 40 tonnes fully loaded.
Tesla Europe posted the numbers today, days before the company plans to formally launch the Semi in Europe at the IAA Transportation show in Hannover.
The European Semi specs
Tesla Europe laid out the figures in a post on X:
- Up to 550 km of range at 40 tonnes, fully loaded
- 1 kWh/km energy consumption
- Megacharger at up to 800 kW, recovering ~60% of range in 30 minutes
- ePTO up to 25 kW
- 40-tonne gross combination weight, 9,100 kg curb weight
The post points to Tesla’s German website for the Tesla Semi and comes ahead of Tesla’s confirmed European launch at IAA Transportation, running September 15-20 in Hannover. Tesla still hasn’t given European pricing or an on-sale date.
How Europe compares to the US
The headline number is range, and it’s lower than what Tesla advertises in the US. The American Long Range Semi is rated at 500 miles (805 km) on an 822 kWh battery. The European figure of 550 km is quoted at 40 tonnes fully loaded, a heavier gross weight than the 82,000 lb (37.2 tonnes) Tesla uses for its US rating. Europe lets zero-emission trucks run above the standard 40-tonne limit, and a heavier load eats range.
But there’s a catch in the curb weight. At 9,100 kg (~20,000 lb), the European Semi is lighter than the US Long Range truck (~23,000 lb) and lands right on the US Standard Range spec of under 20,000 lb. A lighter truck usually means a smaller battery. So the 550 km figure may reflect a standard-range pack rather than the 500-mile Long Range version, something worth pinning down when Tesla shows the truck in Hannover.
Charging is the other gap. Tesla quotes 800 kW for Europe, recovering about 60% of range in half an hour. In the US, Tesla has shown the Semi charging at 1.2 MW, pulling back ~70% in 30 minutes. The efficiency figure lines up: 1 kWh/km is roughly 1.6 kWh per mile, close to the real-world consumption US fleets have logged.
A crowded European market
Tesla isn’t early here. Mercedes-Benz, Volvo Trucks, MAN, Scania, DAF and Renault all sell battery-electric heavy trucks in Europe, with service networks already in place. Mercedes’ eActros 600 offers around 500 km of range on a 600 kWh battery, so Tesla’s 550 km at 40 tonnes is competitive on paper but not a runaway lead.
Tesla is still building the Semi only at its new high-volume factory next to Gigafactory Nevada. Whether European trucks get imported from Nevada or built locally is one of the open questions for Hannover.
CEO Elon Musk has previously said that Tesla will build the semi truck at its Berlin factory.
Electrek’s Take
Top comment by dashpool
I think Volvo's electric trucks are currently the range kings in Europe; claiming 700km of range on a 780kWh pack.
Tesla is presumably just offering the shorter-cab version ("day cab", I think) with less range in Europe because the longer one wouldn't meet maximum length requirements with a normal trailer attached.
Not clear there is much of an efficiency advantage any more; traditional truck makers have had a decade to get their drivetrain tech sorted out.
I'm pretty sure Tesla is using NMC cells, which seems a brave choice in this role. Be interesting to see how they stand up to being cycled a few times a day.
The specs are solid, but the story is what Tesla left out. No price, no delivery date, and no clarity on which battery configuration Europe is actually getting. That curb weight points to a standard range or modified version for EU standards: 9,100 kg is Standard Range territory, which would explain why 550 km comes in well under the 805 km Tesla markets in the US. If that’s the case, European fleets are looking at a shorter-range truck than the spec sheet suggests.
The 800 kW charging cap is also interesting. A big part of the Semi’s pitch is turning a driver’s 30-minute break into a near-full charge, and 800 kW is a real step down from the 1.2 MW Tesla has demonstrated. That’s probably about Europe’s Megacharger rollout and the megawatt charging standard, not the truck itself, but it changes the duty-cycle math for long-haul operators.
Tesla is walking into a market where Volvo and Mercedes have been selling electric trucks for years and already have depots, financing and service sorted. If Tesla can shake up the market, I think it’s with pricing.

title: Kia deploys 200 PV5 electric vans for mail delivery
content:
Peter Johnson
| Sep 11 2026 - 7:11 am PT
Kia developed a custom
for mail delivery. Starting this month, Kia will begin deploying 200 electric vans to post offices.
Kia develops custom PV5 for mail delivery
Following a pilot test, Kia announced Friday that it plans to supply 200 custom electric vans to
The Korea Post
for mail delivery.
Kia deployed customized PV5 Cargo vans to nine regional post offices across South Korea to gather feedback from mail carriers in real-life conditions.
Using suggestions from people who would actually use them, Kia modified the electric van to make loading and unloading easier.
Through a PBV conversion partnership, the custom PV5 features door-damage prevention, an aluminum cargo floor, and a flat cargo area to open up interior space.
“This supply is an example of going beyond simply providing vehicles to realize a PBV perfectly suited to the job by actively reflecting the voices from actual postal delivery sites,” an official from Kia’s domestic business division said.
Kia PV5 mail delivery van (Source: Hyundai Motor Group)
The new partnership is more than just a supply contract. Kia plans to support
The Korea Post’s
transition to electrification with EV training, customized charging solutions, and maintenance.
Kia announced during its PBV Production Hub Tech Day event this week that it now offers
10 different PV5
body styles.
Going forward, Kia will continue developing custom EV solutions for various public services. While it started with the PV5 Passenger and Cargo models, the company is introducing new body styles, including the Open Bed, WAV, Chassis Cab Donor, and Prime variants.
Kia PV5 mail delivery vans (Source: Hyundai Motor Group)
The company is also expanding PBV partnerships in various industries, including with Korea Electric Power Corp, Coupang Partners Association, and GeoYoung.
Through the first eight months of 2026, Kia sold over 39,000 PV5 vans globally. Next week, Kia will reveal
the larger PV7
at IAA Transportation, its second PBV electric van.
Kia said there is “continuous interest” in the larger electric van and that it has already been receiving local inquiries.

title: Geely TT launches at $19,100 — half the price of a Tesla
content:
Fred Lambert
| Sep 11 2026 - 5:40 am PT
Geely launched its new TT electric sport sedan in China, starting at 129,900 yuan (about $19,100), with 800V fast charging and LiDAR on every trim.
That price puts a 640 km sedan with next-generation charging hardware at roughly half the price of a Tesla.
Sold as the Galaxy TT in China and simply “the TT” in Geely’s international materials, the car arrives in five versions: four rear-wheel-drive trims and one all-wheel-drive Ultra. The RWD range runs from 129,900 yuan to 159,900 yuan ($19,100 to $23,500), and the limited-edition Ultra tops out at 185,900 yuan (around $27,300).
Geely says the TT pulled in more than 20,000 pre-orders in about two weeks before launch, so there was demand waiting for it.
The specs don’t match the price
On paper, nothing about the TT reads like a $19,100 car.
Every trim uses an 800V architecture paired with a CATL “Shenxing TT” lithium iron phosphate battery rated for up to 6C charging. Geely claims the system adds close to 500 km of range in 11 minutes. The entry car carries a 63.8 kWh pack good for 640 km on China’s CLTC cycle (518 km WLTP), and a 75.2 kWh version stretches the flagship RWD trim to 725 km CLTC.
The single-motor cars make 245 kW (329 hp). The dual-motor Ultra makes a combined 425 kW (570 hp) and runs 0–100 km/h in 3.8 seconds, with a chassis tuned by Lotus and a “Handling by Lotus” badge on each car. Geely also had the TT set a Guinness World Record for the longest continuous wet-road drift, at more than 46 km.
LiDAR is standard across the lineup, feeding Geely’s G-ASD driver-assistance system for highway and city navigation. Inside, there’s a “Super Eva” AI assistant, a 23-speaker Flyme Sound system, and a flat rear floor in a cabin stretched over a 2,920 mm wheelbase on a car that’s just shy of five meters long.
Priced to go straight at Xiaomi
The comparison Geely wants you to make is with the Xiaomi SU7.
Xiaomi’s new-generation SU7 starts at 229,900 yuan (about $31,870) in China. The TT starts at 129,900 yuan. That’s a 100,000 yuan gap on the entry car, and even the loaded Ultra undercuts a base SU7. Geely is selling a similar-size, similar-mission electric sedan for a little more than half the money.
It’s built on Geely’s GEA EVO platform, with double-wishbone front and five-link rear suspension and adaptive damping. This is the same company that’s been showing off a
500 Wh/kg solid-state battery it plans to pilot in 2027
, and whose brands just
aced Euro NCAP crash testing
alongside GAC and Leapmotor. The cheap price isn’t coming from a cheap car.
For now, the TT is a China-only product. But Geely has already said it plans to
enter the US EV market within two to three years
, and it’s in
advanced talks to take over a Ford plant in Europe

title: Latvenergo expands Baltic battery storage, solar push alongside wind deals - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Latvenergo is folding solar and battery assets into a broader wind-acquisition drive as part of its push to diversify Baltic power generation and strengthen regional energy security.
Brian Publicover
11 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Latvenergo, Latvia’s state-owned utility, is evaluating the acquisition of up to 250 MW of wind or hybrid power projects, adding to a Baltic portfolio that already includes a 265 MW completed solar park and a growing pipeline of battery storage assets.
It said the acquisition search, advised by PricewaterhouseCoopers, forms part of its medium-term strategy to expand renewable generation, diversify its power mix, and strengthen energy security in Latvia and the wider Baltic region.
The company said it will evaluate both ready-to-build projects and operational wind turbines no older than five years, and will proceed to acquisition discussions with developers of the most suitable projects.
It completed the 265 MW Aizpute solar park in Latvia in 2025 and began generating electricity by the first quarter of 2026. According to its half-year results, seven battery storage projects totaling 233.4 MW and 551.2 MWh were under development as of the end of June, while two smaller BESS projects totaling 10.6 MW and 21.9 MWh had already been completed.
Latvenergo also noted a smaller hybrid project at Priekule, comprising an 11.5 MW wind farm under construction, a 9 MW solar plant, and a 2 MW battery storage system already in operation. It didn’t disclose the battery’s energy capacity, a commissioning date, or how the project would participate in the market.
The group claims its development potential runs up to 2,300 MW long-term, but that’s a post-2030 ceiling rather than a near-term target. Its current medium-term strategy calls for 600 MW of new wind and solar by 2026, and its approved Baltic renewable portfolio had reached 1,144 MW by the first half of 2026 – 937 MW newly built and 207 MW under construction.
It acquired the 124 MW Telšiai wind farm in Lithuania from developer Utilitas Wind in May 2024. The project uses 20 Vestas turbines, cost roughly €200 million ($231.7 million) to build, and is set to host a 28.51 MW/57.02 MWh battery storage system.
It also acquired the 147 MW Pienava wind farm in Latvia from Swedish developer Eolus; according to Latvenergo’s half-year report, construction of all foundations at the site had been completed by the end of June, with substations, electrical infrastructure and turbine component installation underway. The 109 MW Laflora Energy wind project began generating electricity during the same period, the corporate report said.
Latvenergo’s acquisition push comes amid a broader pattern of utility-led consolidation in the Baltic renewable energy market, with state-backed utilities acquiring projects from private developers. According to KPMG data, the Baltic states recorded 62 M&A transactions in the most recent 12-month period, marking a modest decline from the prior period.
The Baltic states disconnected from the Russian-controlled electricity grid in February 2025 and synchronized with the Continental European grid, a shift that has increased the strategic importance of domestic and regional generation capacity in the region. Latvenergo has explicitly tied its expansion strategy to this energy-security context.
Separately, Latvenergo said on Sept. 3 that it had joined 13 other energy companies and organizations from nine Baltic Sea countries, including Vestas, Siemens Energy and Eesti Energia’s Enefit, in forming the Baltic Energy Initiative, a cross-border platform aimed at cooperation on offshore wind, hydrogen, carbon transport and storage, and energy infrastructure security across the region.
The Riga-based group first outlined ambitions to become a leading player in the
Baltic BESS market
in February 2025, when it announced plans to install 250 MW/500 MWh of storage by 2030 across its existing hydro and combined-heat-and-power sites, beginning with installations at its CHPP-1 plant, Riga HPP, and CHPP-2. The latest acquisition push extends that storage-and-generation buildout into third-party wind and hybrid assets as well.

title: Lebanon issues new provisions for solar up to 1.5 MW - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Lebanon has introduced new permitting and safety rules for PV systems up to 1.5 MW, establishing municipal oversight and technical requirements for installations.
Emiliano Bellini
11 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Residential
PV project in Beirut
Lebanon’s Ministry of Interior and Municipalities, Ministry of Public Works and Transport, and Ministry of Energy and Water have issued
new rules
for the deployment of PV systems with capacities of up to 1.5 MW.
The government said the interim provisions will remain in force until the country’s regulator introduces final rules, which are currently under development.
Under the new framework, PV systems below 1.5 MW do not require approval from the Ministry of Energy and Water. However, installations must follow a defined municipal administrative and safety procedure.
Municipalities are responsible for verifying compliance with administrative, planning, structural and safety requirements. Structural and electrical or electromechanical engineers must sign off on projects and supervise installation. Upon completion, the engineers must confirm that the systems comply with applicable safety requirements.
Approvals are generally valid for one year, during which installation must be completed.
The government said the new rules are intended to formalize the permitting process for distributed solar installations while strengthening public safety requirements. They also assign responsibilities to engineers involved in PV projects, including oversight of structural and electrical aspects and verification of compliance upon completion.
Lebanon’s cumulative solar capacity reached 1,505 MW at the end of 2025, according to figures published by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), up from 1,081 MW a year earlier.

title: Array Technologies triples its U.S. manufacturing footprint - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The Albuquerque solar tracker manufacturing facility will employ about 300 people and enable it to bring production in house rather than sourcing components from other suppliers.
Anne Fischer
11 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Manufacturing
Trackers
United States
Solar tracker specialist, Array Technologies, recently opened a new $50 million 216,000 square foot manufacturing facility in Albuquerque, New Mexico, nearly tripling its previous capacity.
Founded more than three decades ago in Albuquerque by Ron Corio, developer of the first solar tracker for the Wattsun concentrator, the company now has 100 GW of trackers deployed worldwide.
“By expanding what we can produce here at home, we are strengthening our supply chain, creating skilled career opportunities and building capabilities that will help us serve our customers for years to come, said Kevin Hostetler, chief executive officer of Array Technologies”
The new facility will enable the company to bring production in house rather than sourcing components from other suppliers. Array reports that several components manufactured at the facility will qualify for the Section 45X Advanced Manufacturing Production Tax Credit.
Exterior photograph of ARRAY Technologies new Atrisco manufacturing facility in Albuquerque, New Mexico. The image shows the buildings main entrance, ARRAY signage, company and government flags, and the surrounding parking and landscaped areas beneath a clear blue sky.
Built around lean manufacturing principles and a culture of continuous improvement, Array said the campus will employ about 300 people in roles such as stamping press operators, tooling and die technicians and process engineers.
The company financed the facility through a public-private partnership that includes $2.5 million from New Mexico’s Local Economic Development Act (LEDA) job-creation fund, as well as $250,000 each in LEDA funding from the City of Albuquerque and Bernalillo County and partial property-tax abatement through an Industrial Revenue Bond.
In addition to manufacturing solar tracking technology and fixed-tilt products, Array also supplies foundation and other balance-of-system solutions, software and services.
Last month
Array Technologies reported a second quarter with $342.1 million in earnings, a 53% increase compared to the first quarter and a record $2.5 billion in orders booked. Also announced in August was the completion of the acquisition of Affordable Wire Management (AWM), a provider of wire management, cable protection, and balance-of-system solutions for utility-scale solar and energy storage projects.

title: Solarize Africa: The case of Madagascar - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Madagascar’s diesel-dependent power system faces high costs and chronic blackouts, making solar PV and battery storage an increasingly attractive route to reliable, affordable electrification. Five solar-diesel hybrid projects demonstrate that PV can significantly reduce fuel consumption and electricity prices, offering a scalable model for Madagascar and wider sub-Saharan Africa.
Becquerel Institute
11 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Aerial view of Mananara Central
Africa is too wide to be summarized as a single market, and that’s a common mistake made by many, especially in the northern hemisphere. However, one aspect of solar in Africa applies to the entire continent: its tremendous solar resource. From the desertic areas of the Sahara to the savanna zones in the south and the lush forests in its center, Africa is never short of solar energy but struggles to deploy PV as fast as other continents. The reasons are multiple, from incumbents to financing limitations, from skills to the lack of political willingness (but this is changing fast). But PV development is accelerating beyond the 20 GW installed at the end of 2025, and the reason is not only the need to acceleration electrification rate, but the tremendous impact of rising oil and gas prices.
The case of Madagascar will be discussed here: an island nation in the Indian Ocean, faces one of the most severe energy crises in Africa. With an extremely low electrification rate (depending on the interpretation of numbers, as little as 14% of the population could be considered electrified), most of its population relies on a mix of hydropower systems and diesel generators—a costly and unsustainable solution. The high price of oil, compounded by logistical challenges in transporting fuel across the country’s rugged terrain, has made electricity prohibitively expensive. Main local utility Jirama operates at a loss, as government-imposed price caps prevent them from passing the full cost of generation onto consumers. The result? Electricity is frequently rationed, with many communities experiencing blackouts for several hours each day.
Political unrest at the end of 2025, that led to the exile of the former president André Rajoelina and a temporary takeover by the army was driven by recurring rolling blackouts, as well as water shortages, managed by the very same utility. While we won’t focus on the latest, aging infrastructure and uncompetitive electricity costs are a permanent burden for minority of the population with access to electricity.
In this context, a consortium of several companies, driven by Enerdeal, now a Belgian subsidiary of Portuguese utility EDP, Becquerel Institute and several additional players have developed a series of solar hybridization projects in the country aimed at integrating solar PV systems—and in some cases, battery storage—with existing diesel generators.
These projects, implemented in five locations, offer a glimpse into how renewable energy can reduce costs, improve reliability, and pave the way for a more sustainable energy future in Madagascar, and at large in sub-Saharan Africa.
This paper explores the technical, economic, and social implications of these projects, as well as the broader lessons they hold for electrification efforts across Africa, based on the lessons learnt from these solar projects from 2016 to 2026.
Madagascar’s energy crisis: A background
Madagascar’s low electrification rate remains among the lowest in the world. In rural areas, access to electricity is scarce, forcing communities to rely on kerosene lamps, diesel generators, and a variety of small solar home systems. Or simply no electricity at all. Even in urban centers, the grid is unreliable and expensive, with frequent power cuts disrupting daily life, businesses, and education. Some days, cuts can amount to 8 days per day or more, plunging entire neighborhoods of the capital city Antananarivo in the dark.
Equipment has been adapted to the blackouts and small LED bulbs with several hours of battery storage are now common in the country, together with small diesel generators in most hotels, restaurants or administrative centers. Small diesel generators are used as backup power in wealthy places.
The primary sources of electricity in Madagascar include hydropower and diesel generators, with a growing share of solar electricity. But the total electricity consumption barely reached 2.5 TWh in the last years, the equivalent of 12% of a city like Brussels for instance, while the country has a population approaching 34 millions. Electrification rate officially reached 40%, if people served by 20W PV modules with a small battery and charging ports for mobile devices are accounted. The real electrification rate is significantly lower, while increasing in recent years.
Most regional cities use electricity through local mini-grids, in general a backbone coming from one or several diesel-powered plants. Diesel-generators are common as central power plants in mini-grids, because of the relatively low investment cost and the existence of local expertise.
The fast development of solar power, pushed by the current government, Jirama and local authorities, is fueled by the need to electrify much faster, but also primarily by high fuel costs of imported oil, with price being even higher in remote locations, due to internal transport costs and additional local “taxes”. The recent geopolitical events having triggered a massive increase in oil prices, this has led to further issues with energy costs. While oil prices also impact road transport, several African countries are moving towards electric mobility. The case of Ethiopia that has banned the import of ICE vehicles is exemplary, while several countries are pushing for a faster electrification of two- and three-wheelers. While this won’t be discussed here, it represents also a driver for fast solar-driven electrification.
In this situation, Solar represents the most obvious solution and is poised to developing fast, because of its versatility (newly with competitive battery storage). Most utility-scale solar plants cover just some MW and complement an existing diesel generator. Battery storage starts being added and is expected to develop fast in the coming years, with the recent importation of components worth hundreds of MW.
As experienced first-hand, PV is sometimes plagued by maintenance issues such as lack of spare parts, missing skills, badly adapted training material from developed countries. This could be solved by smarter training of maintenance teams, standardization of components and better maintenance contract. Incumbents operating diesel plants must be treated with respect and understanding, since solar is obviously reducing their initial business, leading to possible confrontations and limited cooperation. This also can be solved smartly, since adding solar might prove more profitable than the existing plants.
Finally, hydropower exists and could be developed, however limited to a few regions and vulnerable to droughts, which have become more frequent due to climate change. Development times are considerably higher than solar or diesel generators and should represent a long-term investment rather than a short-term solution. However, connecting cities to create large control zones, using hydropower plants to balance PV variability during the rainy season, should be planned and properly financed to drive the electricity grid towards maturity, once electrification has been improved.
The economic and social cost of diesel dependency
The reliance on diesel generators has far-reaching consequences that partially led to the 2025 uprising. In that respect, Madagascar could be considered as one of the first country to experience political unrest due to restrictions in electricity provision.
High diesel prices, especially in the countryside have plagued the local utility Jirama and increased its losses: with retail electricity prices capped for obvious economic and social reasons, the high dependency to oil prices is increasing the losses of the utility for almost each kWh sold. This has created a vicious circle, Jirama can barely invest in upgrades, leading to further deterioration of the grid, not only for electricity but also for its other missions, such as water provision.
Needless to mention the environmental impact: Diesel generators are highly polluting, contributing to air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, but also tremendous noise when installed close to cities.
Social Inequality is a real issue without reliable electricity and improving living conditions of the population requires access to electricity, students struggle to study after dark, businesses face reduced productivity, and healthcare facilities cannot operate life-saving equipment consistently with a back-up diesel generator. It is also estimated that only 2% of the population has access to clean cooking.
The political dimensions of this crisis cannot be ignored as explained before.
Solar hybridization projects: A technical overview
The so-called Finexpo project was aiming at hybridizing diesel generators with solar PV, in order to reduce oil consumption and electricity prices. The project has been financed by the Export authority of the Belgian government, Finexpo, through a long-term loan to the authorities of Madagascar.
The project has been led by a consortium of Belgian and Malagasy companies, from engineering to control and installation, and can be considered as a perfect successful example of multi-cultural work and understanding.
The first takeover of the project is the considerable lead-time due to the need to align positions at government level between the two countries. While the financial scheme can be considered fair, the time from inception to realization was considerably high for a solar project. With 10 years elapsed, solar technology evolved significantly and the project would have been done differently in 2026. International financing needs to be fast-tracked.
Due to financial constraints, the project focused on five remote sites, in mid-size cities (Ambilobe, Mananara, Marovoay) and two touristic islands (Sainte-Marie and Nosy Bé).
Image: Sainte-Marie site
Becquerel Institute
Each of these locations shared a common profile: powered initially by diesel generators at high cost and limited reliability, due to difficulties in transporting oil mostly. A total of 5 MW of PV was added, with the largest plant amounting to 1.5 MW. The systems are configured in islanding mode, managing grid stability with demands often in the range of 300 kW to over 1 MW.
The overarching goal was to reduce diesel consumption by integrating solar PV systems and, in one case, battery storage, into the existing infrastructure. Battery storage could have been used widely and reduced further diesel consumption, would the project have been started later, with declining solar PV and battery costs. One of the plants was equipped with a BESS system, but with reduced capacity compared to an optimal design.
Hybridization involves combining diesel generators with solar PV (and/or batteries) in a way that optimizes efficiency and cost. There are two primary configurations:
Diesel as Master, PV as Slave: The diesel generator runs continuously at a minimum load, typically never below 25-30% of capacity, but in the reality 40% is not uncommon. Solar PV injects electricity when available, reducing the diesel generator’s output. The limitation is clear: If PV plus minimal diesel production exceeds demand, the excess energy is curtailed and wasted, as diesel generators cannot run below their minimum idle threshold. This is the solution that was implemented in these projects.
PV as Master, Diesel as Slave: in this configuration, Solar PV takes priority, with diesel generators kicking in only when PV production is insufficient. To run smoothly, this solution requires battery storage to smooth out fluctuations in PV output and avoid as much as possible to have to restart diesel generators. This solution would be now more acceptable, with battery storage allowing to maintain the solar+BESS system operational at almost all times and maintaining the diesel generators in reserve for specific period of the year when solar+BESS combined would require too much capex to be dimensioned at the right size.
The projects yielded encouraging results: the reduction in diesel consumption was significant and the decline of the cost of end consumers followed. Solar PV displaced a significant portion of diesel-generated electricity, particularly during daylight hours, but also, thanks to storage during the evening consumption peak. Average electricity price declined by half in average, depending on the configuration and most could be achievable with additional investments, especially in battery storage.
Image: Mananara Central
Becquerel Institute
Broader implications: Why this matters for Madagascar and Africa
The project highlights a critical truth: energy access is not just an economic issue—it is a social and political one. The 2025 political upheaval in Madagascar was, in a large part, a rejection of energy poverty. The new temporary government has signaled a commitment to accelerating electrification, particularly through solar and storage, with considerable investments and pressure put on existing players.
The plummeting cost of solar PV and batteries has made hybrid systems increasingly viable and represent today the fastest path to electrification. Easier to deploy than large-scale hydropower or wind projects, solar and batteries offer the possibility to be temporarily added to diesel generators, reducing significantly their use of fossil fuels.
Hybridization will allow for downsizing diesel capacity, but economic consequences must be managed properly by local governments, since the economy of oil is central in many African countries and requires to be addressed carefully and smartly. Diesel will remain necessary for electricity production in remote places, allowing temporarily to stabilize mini grids with high solar and battery storage without significant additional investments. Priority should be given to electrification through solar PV, optimizing existing resources to maximize solar deployment, rather than looking for the optimum 24/7 zero-carbon solution. This will come in a second phase, but electrification is a moral challenge in most sub-Saharan African countries.
A key challenge to scaling up solar PV in African countries remains administrative and regulatory hurdles. Slow approval of new projects could be fast tracked, and while respecting the rights of everyone, be given priorities in courts and administration. Financing also requires accelerated procedures.
Political will is critical—energy access is not just about technology, but equity and development are now a cornerstone of policies in many African countries. This has been made obvious also for the
International Solar Alliance
during its last African Regional Committee Meeting in Zimbabwe last august: the political commitment is there, money is available, skills remain to be built.
The question now is not whether Africa and Madagascar can transition to renewable energy, but how quickly it can do so. With the right policies, investments, and PV-based technical solutions, the entire continent could leapfrog the diesel era and embrace a cleaner, more affordable solar-driven energy future.
Becquerel Institute
is a strategic consulting and applied research company specialising in solar photovoltaics and energy transition. Founded in Brussels in 2014, with regional offices in France, Italy and Spain, it provides strategic advice across all segments of the PV value chain including market trends, analysis of development conditions and political and regulatory frameworks, assessment of production costs, etc. Becquerel Institute applies this expertise to support companies in Europe, America, Asia and Africa, and is a recognised partner in European and international research projects. The company also actively supports international organisations and associations.

title: 'I make a point of thanking people for asking critical questions and disagreeing openly' - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
This week, Women in Solar+ Europe gives voice to Hanna König, Head of Division Project Execution, at Germany’s Enertrag SE. She says the most important element of an inclusive organisational culture is ensuring that everyone feels safe to contribute ideas and opinions, particularly when they disagree with the majority or with people in more senior positions.
Women in Solar+ Europe
11 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Hannah König
Every industry benefits from diversity, not just ours. What makes it particularly important and urgent for the solar and renewable energy industries is the lack of qualified professionals. We need specific competencies, including electrical engineering expertise, that are scarce by nature. Expanding the talent pool as widely as possible is therefore vital to our economic growth.
Making sure that everyone feels welcome is a matter of economic success just as much as it is a matter of human values. We cannot afford to overlook capable people when our industries need such a broad range of skills to deliver the energy transition. Inclusion must allow us to attract talent from across society and create the conditions for everyone to contribute effectively.
Looking beyond identity
I have not observed the major shifts in gender-inclusive leadership that I had hoped to see. What I have observed are individuals genuinely making an impact because they excelled in their positions and supported those who delivered results, without paying specific attention to gender. Their focus was on recognising people’s abilities and contributions.
In my personal experience, some of those who spoke most about gender equality focused primarily on differences and, in doing so, sometimes reinforced the very biases they sought to challenge. Only when we look beyond gender, age and other aspects of identity can we universally appreciate people for who they are and for what they contribute to a company.
For me, DEI should mean that every human being has the same opportunities and is measured by the same standards. One of the biggest challenges at executive level is that the inclusion of specific groups is often misunderstood as the exclusion of others. Many executive leaders are still men, and some may feel threatened by a programme that appears to promote women while leaving them outside the conversation.
This is one reason why such initiatives can struggle to secure leadership buy-in. The lack of executive support, often cited as one of the greatest barriers to DEI programmes, may sometimes be the understandable resistance of someone who feels excluded. If inclusion is the objective, the way we design and communicate these programmes must reflect that principle.
Creating safety for disagreement
The most important element of an inclusive organisational culture is ensuring that everyone feels safe to contribute ideas and opinions, particularly when they disagree with the majority or with people in more senior positions. Each of us is limited in our individual perception and thinking. Only when different perspectives come together do we have the opportunity to see a fuller picture.
I make a point of thanking people for asking critical questions and disagreeing openly. Consistency is essential because employees may remember one negative reaction from a leader more clearly than ten positive ones. Leaders cannot invite challenge only when it is comfortable; they must demonstrate repeatedly that thoughtful disagreement is valued.
I am also open about my own mistakes. Only when we address mistakes can we learn from them. A leader’s willingness to acknowledge being wrong signals that uncertainty and imperfection do not need to be hidden, and that honest reflection is part of how an organisation improves.
Leadership requires clarity
One of the most important leadership lessons I have learned is not to become too distracted by what other people might think of you. You cannot control their opinions; you can control only your own mindset and behaviour. I believe this is important for anyone striving to become a leader.
Wanting to be liked by everyone will limit your effectiveness. As a leader, you are responsible for a company and for everyone working within it, and that responsibility sometimes requires difficult choices. Early in my career, I had to dismiss someone because their behaviour was disrupting the team. Experiences like this teach you to be clear about what really matters and to act accordingly.
Make being different your advantage
The renewable energy industry is young and therefore more diverse than the traditional fossil fuel industry. Even so, as a young woman entering the sector, there is still a good chance that you will find yourself in a room full of men. My advice is to treat that difference as an advantage.
Being different means that you stand out and that people are more likely to remember you. What they remember, however, is your choice. Prepare carefully for what you want that impression to be. Focus on your strengths, build your knowledge and make sure that your contribution is what stays with them.
Hannah König is an experienced executive and energy expert with more than 15 years of international experience in the energy sector. She currently serves as Head of Project Execution at Enertrag, where she is responsible for the global execution of projects in wind energy, solar PV, battery storage and electrolysis, leading an international team of more than 90 employees. Previously, she held senior leadership positions at Energy Infrastructure Partners and EnBW, with responsibility for investments, major infrastructure projects and strategic procurement. Her experience spans the entire energy value chain – from project development and investment decisions to implementation and operations. She also brings experience from supervisory and board roles. Since 2026, she has served as a member of the Board of Directors of EBL.

title: Sunny north and cloudy south as Super El Niño defines South American winter - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In a new weekly update for
pv magazine
, Solcast, a DNV company, reports that Super El Niño drove a sharp north–south irradiance divide across South America in winter 2026, with sunnier conditions in the north and persistent cloud reducing solar irradiance across much of the south. Two rare August snowstorms in Chile’s Atacama Desert also caused likely snow-related losses for solar PV assets, alongside severe rainfall, flooding, and mudslides.
pv magazine
11 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
This year’s escalating super El Niño produced a clear north-south divide in South American irradiance during winter 2026, according to analysis using the
Solcast API
. Northern areas were generally sunnier than usual, while persistent cloud reduced irradiance farther south. Separately, two rare August snow events in the Atacama Desert created likely snow- related losses for solar assets in the region.
The winter pattern was broadly consistent with conditions typically associated with El Niño in South America: drier weather in the north and wetter weather toward the south. Southern Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay and northern Argentina experienced the wetter conditions associated with the event, although these effects more commonly emerge later in the year. El Niño was officially declared by several national weather agencies at the beginning of winter, with NOAA declaring the event on June 11 and Brazil’s Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia including it in its June bulletin. It has continued to strengthen rapidly, recording the fastest rise in the Relative Niño 3.4 indicator on record.
In comparison to 2015, the last time we saw El Niño for all three months winter, 2026 has a much larger deviations from normal with both greater irradiance losses and gains across the continent which may be the result of the stronger El Niño this year. Broad patterns remain the same however with lower than usual irradiance in most of Argentina, Chile, Paraguay and Uruguay, and sunnier conditions in northern Brazil. In contrast, 2026 was more uniformly sunnier in the northern part of the continent and gifted eastern Brazil with some extra sun.
Snow first reached the Atacama Desert shortly before mid-August. Around 20 August, a cutoff low brought a second round of snow. That storm also produced intense rainfall elsewhere in northern Chile, with some areas receiving multiple years’ worth of rain over several days. The resulting mudslides and flash flooding prompted the Chilean president to declare a state of emergency.
Modelling for a representative 100 MW PV plant in the Atacama Desert shows how the two snowfall periods would align with estimated snow-related losses during August.
The north-south contrast strengthened through winter, with similar patterns of above- and below-average irradiance in July and August. La Costa recorded the largest positive anomaly after three consistently sunnier-than-usual months, with some areas finishing more than 30% above average. Persistent cloud left most of Argentina 15% to 20% below average. Brazil was more mixed, although northern and eastern regions ended the season sunnier than average, while all but the south recorded above-average irradiance in August.
Chile did not follow a single pattern. Northern areas moved from a sunnier June to cloudier conditions in July and August. Chilean Patagonia moved in the opposite direction, with sunnier conditions in both months as Super El Niño disrupted the usual westerly winds that bring moist air into the region.
produces these figures by tracking clouds and aerosols at 1-2km resolution globally, using satellite data and proprietary
AI/ML algorithms
. This data is used to drive irradiance models, enabling Solcast to calculate irradiance at high resolution, with typical bias of less than 2%, and also cloud-tracking forecasts. This data is used by more than 350 companies managing over 350 GW of solar assets globally.

title: South Korea forecast to add 3.5 GW of solar in 2026 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The Export–Import Bank of Korea says the country is on track to add more this solar this year than last year, as the Korean government works on developing a distributed power grid that facilitates greater integration of distributed energy resources.
Patrick Jowett
11 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Residential
South Korea
Utility-scale
South Korea is expected to install 3.5 GW of solar this year, according to a report from the Korea Eximbank.
The state-owned export credit agency’s report adds the country installed 3.1 GW of solar in 2025, meaning the market is set to grow this year.
The Japan and Republic of Korea programme of the EU Business Hub, an EU-funded incentive supporting small and medium-sized enterprises, told
pv magazine
the Korean government is working on a next-generation distributed power grid to facilitate greater integration of distributed energy resources.
“The government’s next-generation distributed-grid programme is intended to address the integration of distributed energy resources through measures including microgrids,” a statement from the hub explained. “Operators for these projects were due to be selected in the second quarter of 2026 following calls launched in the first quarter.”
A key development in South Korea this year has been the implementation of its
Sunshine Income Villages initiative
, a scheme that will install solar PV facilities on idle land, farmland and reservoirs, with local residents forming cooperatives to participate in the projects via energy and profit sharing.
The first villages to take part in the scheme were selected in August, while a second call has already taken place. The country’s Ministry of Interior and Safety has set a target of identifying 700 solar villages this year, increasing to 2,500 by 2030.
The EU Business Hub added that distribution-grid energy storage systems also feature in the government’s development of a next-generation distributed power grid.
In July, South Korea
signed its first deals
to build energy storage systems directly on distribution lines, through agreements with nine companies totaling 128 MW/640 MWh of energy storage systems across 32 lines in areas where capacity issues have left new solar projects waiting in interconnection queues.
The country is targeting 700 MW of distribution-line energy storage systems by 2030, according to previous reports, which it says would enable an additional 1 GW of renewable interconnection capacity.
Korea Eximbank’s report adds that increased policy support is needed to ensure that expansion of the country’s domestic solar market. The EU Business Hub told
pv magazine
this encompasses “preferential support for domestically produced products, as well as expanding financial support to help Korean companies secure overseas solar projects.”
Earlier this week, South Korea’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment (MCEE) launched a new
solar industry competitiveness committee
centered around rebuilding the country’s domestic solar supply chain.
South Korea is working to reach 100 GW of renewables capacity by the end of the decade, according to its First Renewable Energy Basic Plan published earlier this year, up from about 37.1 GW at the time of the plan’s announcement. The plans calls for roughly 56.2 GW of new solar capacity, split between 12 GW of large grid-connected complexes and 44.2 GW from designated sites including industrial rooftops, agrivoltaic and floating installations, transport corridors and public buildings.
In August, construction got underway on
South Korea’s largest solar complex to date
, a 400 MW solar PV complex to be built on approximately 4.79 million square metres of idle land.

title: Chinese PV Industry Brief: Tongwei clears antitrust hurdle for acquisition of polysilicon competitor Qinghai Lihao - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In other news, Longi said its operating conditions are expected to improve after a CNY 3.68 billion ($542 million) first-half loss, while GCL SI and Ant Digital Technologies agreed to develop an AI-enabled carbon-management platform. JinkoSolar, meanwhile, proposed renaming its overseas parent Jinko Holdings Limited as it expands beyond solar manufacturing into strategic investments.
Vincent Shaw
11 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Tongwei solar cell factory in China.
said it has largely completed auditing, valuation and other due-diligence work for its planned acquisition of a 100% stake in Qinghai Lihao Clean Energy. The company has also received antitrust clearance from China’s State Administration for Market Regulation, removing a key regulatory hurdle for the transaction. Tongwei said in August that the acquisition had entered the final stage of negotiations over the transaction plan. Qinghai Lihao is a privately held joint-stock company registered in 2021 in Xining, Qinghai province. Its business scope includes electronic materials and related manufacturing and trading activities. Industry reports describe Lihao as a rapidly scaling polysilicon producer leveraging Qinghai’s renewable power resources. Public reporting on its buildout indicates that a first-phase 50,000 metric ton polysilicon project reached commissioning in 2022, with longer-term capacity ambitions reported to be significantly higher.
Chairman Zhong Baoshen said at the company’s first-half results briefing on Sept. 3 that its most difficult period had passed and operating conditions were expected to gradually improve. Longi reported a first-half net loss attributable to shareholders of CNY 3.68 billion ($542 million), widening about 43% year on year, although its gross margin returned to positive territory. Back-contact (BC) module sales rose 125% from a year earlier, while overseas markets accounted for more than 65% of module revenue. Zhong said measures to curb excessive competition in China’s solar industry could help stabilize supply-chain prices and support a recovery in profitability.
GCL System Integration (GCL SI)
Ant Digital Technologies
signed an agreement to develop “GCL Carbon Chain 4.0” at the 2026 Inclusion – The Bund Summit on Sept. 11. The companies plan to integrate AI agent technology into the platform to support intelligent operations, proactive decision-making and ecosystem collaboration. The upgraded platform will offer downstream customers services including carbon accounting, carbon asset verification, green electricity trading and green finance. GCL SI aims to expand the system from an internal corporate tool into an open carbon-management infrastructure platform for the wider industry. The company previously worked with Ant Digital on the GCL Carbon Chain blockchain-based supply-chain carbon tracking system.
JinkoSolar Holdings
said on Sept. 9 that its board has approved a proposal to change the company’s English name to Jinko Holdings Limited, alongside a corresponding Chinese name change to Jinko Holdings Co., Ltd. The change applies only to the Cayman Islands-incorporated parent company and will not affect Shanghai-listed JinkoSolar Co., Ltd., while its NYSE ticker will remain JKS. The proposal is subject to shareholder approval at a meeting scheduled for Oct. 21. The company said the change reflects its shift from a pure-play solar manufacturer toward a holding and strategic investment platform. It plans to retain control of its core solar and energy storage businesses while expanding into areas including artificial intelligence, renewable energy, advanced materials and commercial space.

title: The Hydrogen Stream: AEM electrolysis could deliver hydrogen at $3.27/kg, say Repsol, P2HP - pv magazine Global
content:

Power to Hydrogen (P2H2) and Repsol completed a 1,250-hour pilot of P2H2’s hybrid AEM electrolyzer technology, demonstrating operation at 40% to 100% load, pressures up to 30 bar and hydrogen purity of up to 99.9%.
