Power to Hydrogen
(P2H2), a developer of anion exchange membrane (AEM) electrolyzer systems, and Spanish energy company
completed a pilot validating P2H2’s hybrid AEM electrolysis technology for large-scale green hydrogen production. Conducted through Repsol’s All4Zero industrial innovation hub, the program accumulated more than 1,250 hours of parametric and durability testing on a five-cell short stack incorporating commercial-scale cells, including extensive operation under simulated renewable-energy load profiles. Testing covered operation from approximately 40% to 100% load and at pressures ranging from 2 to 30 bar, with hydrogen purity reaching up to 99.9% at 30 bar. According to the companies, the stack met or exceeded key targets for efficiency, dynamic flexibility and durability, while demonstrating an irreversible degradation rate of approximately 2 mV per 1,000 operating hours, which P2H2 says supports a projected stack lifetime of more than 50,000 hours. The company argues that its hybrid AEM architecture can provide PEM-like performance and responsiveness while using a fundamentally lower-cost materials platform, including reduced reliance on scarce platinum-group metals such as iridium. Based on Repsol-specific operating assumptions and the U.S. Department of Energy’s H2A-Lite cost-modeling framework, P2H2 projects a levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH) of approximately €3.86 ($4.47)/kg, around 16% below incumbent electrolyzer technologies, with the potential to fall to approximately €2.82 ($3.27)/kg under optimized renewable-energy scenarios using hybrid power purchase agreements. Importantly, these LCOH figures are modeled projections rather than costs directly demonstrated during the 1,250-hour pilot. Following the results, P2H2 and Repsol are exploring a potential 500 kW-to-MW-scale demonstration as a next step toward commercial deployment.
Indian researchers
have highlighted the importance of elements such as cerium, lanthanum, neodymium and praseodymium in the hydrogen sector, saying their distinctive redox, electronic and oxygen-storage properties can improve catalytic activity, reaction kinetics, stability and hydrogen yields. They said that recycling, recovery and reuse of rare earth elements (REEs) within a circular-economy framework are essential to ensure their use in green hydrogen is sustainable. The researchers from Alagappa University published
their results
Scientific Reviews
Researchers led by
University of Oregon
chemist Paul Kempler have identified dissolved iron impurities as a key factor controlling the degradation of alkaline water electrolyzers during power interruptions. “These findings show that anode degradation during reverse polarization is strongly dependent on the shutdown duration and the retention of iron in the catalyst. When minimizing the shutdown time is impractical, electrolyte engineering through tuning the dissolved metal content may offer a solution,” the researchers said in “
Reverse polarization degradation of nickel iron oxyhydroxide anodes in alkaline water electrolysis
,” published in
Chem Catalysis
A team at the
Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)
has demonstrated an electrochemical method to extract pure hydrogen gas from hydrogen carrier molecules, which the researchers said could improve process efficiency. The system couples a palladium-based separation membrane with a hydrogen-generating electrode via a molten hydroxide electrolyte. “The separation membrane selectively transports hydrogen while preventing other components of the reaction mixture from passing through,” the researchers said. Ammonia is first dehydrogenated using a catalyst containing ruthenium and cesium. The resulting hydrogen then reaches the separation membrane, with its opposite side in contact with the molten hydroxide electrolyte. “The electrochemical gradient across this membrane effectively creates a ‘vacuum’ for hydrogen, providing a strong driving force for its transport across the membrane. It also converts the hydrogen into protons and electrons, which travel separately through the molten electrolyte and external circuit, respectively, before recombining at a second electrode to form hydrogen gas,” the researchers said. They added that the approach eliminates the need for a separate downstream hydrogen purification process.

The organization said the discovered hydrogen has a mole fraction comparable to some of the world’s highest-purity natural hydrogen reservoirs, setting a new record for natural hydrogen content in China. The mole fraction – the ratio of the number of moles of hydrogen to the total number of moles of all substances in a mixture – ranges from 97.33% to 98.24% in the Sichuan Basin deposit. According to
China Hydrogen Alliance

title: China wafer prices fall as August rally fades, polysilicon outlook remains uncertain - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In a new weekly update for
pv magazine
, OPIS, a Dow Jones company, provides a quick look at the main price trends in the global PV industry.
11 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
According to the OPIS Global Solar Markets Report released on Sept. 8, Free-On-Board (FOB) China M10 and 210R wafer prices fell to $0.149/pc and $0.156/pc, respectively, down 1.97% and 2.50% week on week.
The wafer price rally seen in mid-August has failed to sustain momentum, with prices returning to a downward trend.
Industry sources said n-type 183 wafers, which had risen notably on a temporary surge in overseas demand and reached transaction prices above CNY 1.10 ($0.164)/pc at the peak, fell back to around CNY 1/pc this week, with some transactions reportedly below that level.
One trade participant attributed the decline primarily to weakening downstream demand, which has left wafer suppliers with little choice but to lower prices to facilitate sales. Another pointed to suppliers’ weak negotiating position, noting that buyers now commonly close deals several cents per piece below manufacturers’ initial offers.
Despite the weaker market, operating rates across wafer producers have remained largely unchanged, as the market watches how the upstream polysilicon market develops following last week’s reported production-cut agreement, according to a specialized wafer manufacturer.
The agreement refers to an industry meeting held in Sichuan last week involving the China Photovoltaic Industry Association and major polysilicon manufacturers, which industry sources said was aimed at launching a production-control initiative. The initiative reportedly targets total 2026 polysilicon output of 1.0-1.1 million metric tons (MT), an approximate 20% reduction from 2025 output, with the same target maintained for 2027.
The meeting reportedly also called for around 500,000 MT of capacity across Sichuan, Yunnan and Qinghai to suspend production and undergo technological upgrades in the fourth quarter, with participating manufacturers required to sign agreements committing to production cuts. Although a source at a leading polysilicon manufacturer confirmed that the meeting took place, its specific details and outcomes have not been officially verified.
Another source questioned the likely effectiveness of the initiative, noting that the agreement’s legal enforceability remains uncertain and that the reported annual output target would still be sufficient to meet end-market demand. The source added that the planned fourth-quarter suspensions and upgrades are primarily aimed at reducing energy consumption to comply with national standards. Without actual capacity exit, the source said, the other efforts appear somewhat superficial.
With the polysilicon price outlook still uncertain, some wafer manufacturers are seeking to lower raw-material costs by sourcing material for near-term delivery from the futures market at around CNY 37/kg and supplementing it with lower-grade spot material, industry sources said.
Polysilicon production, meanwhile, continues to rise. Domestic output reached around 118,900 MT in August, up 13.1% month over month, according to the Silicon Branch of the China Nonferrous Metals Industry Association. Based on manufacturers’ production plans, September output is expected to rise further to around 124,000 MT, up approximately 4.4%.
The high-water season in major production regions is nearing its end, however, bringing a period of abundant hydropower and lower electricity costs to a close. One market source said this makes September the final opportunity for polysilicon producers to increase output and build inventories ahead of the low-water season. Industry sources said some wafer manufacturers may also be forced to reduce production as the low-water season begins in October.
According to industry feedback, operating rates at leading wafer manufacturers are currently around 50%, compared with nearly 70% at major specialized producers. Second-tier manufacturers are generally operating at around 30%-40%.
Leading wafer manufacturers are currently making only modest price reductions, one industry source said, but output cuts in the fourth quarter could give them more leverage to support prices.

OPIS APAC Solar Weekly Report

title: Underwater solar cells achieve operational stability 30 feet below the surface
content: Researchers at Yunnan University and Southwest United Graduate School have demonstrated functional underwater solar cells operating at a depth of 10 meters (33 feet) in the South China Sea. The achievement smashes previous limits. Earlier attempts to harvest solar energy underwater stalled out in shallow waters under two meters deep, where sunlight is still plentiful but practical applications are scarce. Combined with an estimated continuous operational lifespan of roughly 5.5 years, this technology could ultimately offer a reliable, long-term power source for remote oceanic systems. The study shows that submerged photovoltaics can provide a viable power source for underwater sensors, cameras, and communication systems in the future. “Very few studies have been reported on underwater solar cells, and all of them are focused on very shallow water depths of only two meters or less, a scenario far from catering for requirements of practical application,” said Wen-Hua Zhang, the study author. “This work presents the first functional validation of submerged solar cells practically operating at a water depth of up to about 10 meters, greatly broadening their application scope,” Zhang added. Bandgap optimization Standard commercial silicon solar cells are designed to capture broad terrestrial sunlight, particularly red/infrared rays. Underwater, silicon cells lose most of their efficiency. Typically, submerged solar cells struggle to harvest energy due to the rapid loss of sunlight intensity underwater, posing a hurdle for marine monitoring applications like aquaculture. To address this, Zhang’s team designed wide-bandgap solar cells optimized to capture the blue-to-orange light wavelengths that penetrate ocean waters best. By capturing ambient light beneath the waves, underwater solar cells present a transformative solution to the long-standing power limitations of marine technology. Generating 324 mWh of electricity in just two hours at a depth of 10 meters, these cells produce sufficient energy to recharge standard lithium-ion batteries. Submerged solar cells provide a self-sustaining power source for environmental sensors, monitoring cameras, and communication hardware far from the coastline, doing away with costly wired connections and constant battery replacements. The schematic diagram of submerged perovskite solar cells for underwater applications. Credit: Simin Ma, Yunnan University Shows promise in testing Tested under simulated conditions, these specialized cells proved exceptionally durable, retaining roughly 96 percent of their efficiency after 300 days of storage. Plus, the prototype cells showed almost zero degradation over 1,160 hours at a simulated depth of 10 meters off the Weizhou Islands in the South China Sea. “What surprised us most was so much electrical energy our large-area modules generated under real-world conditions at 10-meter water depth for only two hours,” noted Zhang. “Moreover, we have achieved scaling from small‑area laboratory cells to large‑size modules. The combination of the laboratory investigations and the in-field experiments provides strong evidence for the operation of underwater photovoltaics,” said Zhang. Among the future challenges, these cells must pair high durability with crystal-clear light transmission to remain effective for long durations. Also, underwater solar deployment requires overcoming extreme conditions such as corrosive salt , high pressure, and water ingress. Next, the team plans to push deeper into the dark, testing how far down solar technology can go while laying the groundwork for standardized testing protocols for underwater photovoltaics. The study was published in the journal Joule.

title: US submarine captured in Iran, can operate at 20,000-feet ocean depth
content: Iran has claimed that it captured an American underwater drone, according to reports. The underwater vehicle was captured near the Strait of Hormuz by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.Reports claimed that the captured vehicle closely matches Anduril Dive-LD underwater drone.Dive-LD can conduct Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance missions. The drone is also capable of performing mine warfare and precision placement missions.Underwater vehicle can autonomously conduct missions for upto 10 daysThe vehicle can autonomously conduct missions for upto 10 days. The drone integrates open software, mechanical, and electrical interfaces, which allow for seamless integration and rapid configuration of multiple payloads and sensors at a time – delivering relevant, impactful, and affordable capability.The vehicle is capable of conducting missions at 6,000-meters ocean depth. Anduril also claimed that the Dive-LD combines exceptional payload flexibility, low logistics, and superior performance to enable a wide range of defense and commercial missions.On September 8, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced that it had seized an American unmanned underwater vehicle near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz. Photographs released by Iranian sources show a vehicle that closely resembles the Dive-LD, an autonomous underwater system developed by US defense company Anduril. Autonomous underwater vehicles can undertake extended missionsThe incident is significant not simply because an unmanned vehicle was lost, but because underwater drones are becoming an increasingly important part of naval operations. Unlike conventional submarines, autonomous underwater vehicles can undertake extended missions without placing a crew directly in danger.The vehicle is approximately 5.8 metres long, around 1.2 metres in diameter and weighs roughly three tonnes. It is designed for long-duration operations and can reportedly operate at depths of up to 6,000 metres, depending on configuration and mission requirements.One of the most important characteristics of systems such as the Dive-LD is their flexibility. An AUV can be configured with different sensors and payloads depending on the mission. This allows a single basic platform to perform a variety of tasks without requiring a traditional crewed submarine.For navies, that creates an attractive proposition: relatively small unmanned vehicles can be sent into dangerous waters to gather information, survey the seabed or search for mines without risking sailors.Instead of putting dozens of sailors aboard a submarine, a navy can deploy unmanned vehicles to perform specific missions. Some can be relatively inexpensive compared with crewed submarines, while others are designed for much longer-range and more complex operations.The United States and its allies are investing heavily in this concept. Anduril, for example, is developing larger autonomous underwater systems alongside smaller vehicles such as the Dive-LD. Australia is also pursuing the Ghost Shark extra-large autonomous underwater vehicle program with Anduril.

title: USAF tests nuclear missile readiness in surprise drone threat exercise
content: The US Air Force has tested how quickly its nuclear missile force can transition from routine operations to a high-pressure combat scenario, conducting a four-day, no-notice exercise that included a simulated drone threat and the recapture of a missile launch facility.Called Sentinel Dragon 26-02, the commander-directed exercise ran from August 4 to 7, 2026, across units of the Air Force’s 20th Air Force. Unlike a conventional large-scale exercise, most participating personnel were given no advance warning.The setup was designed to show commanders how operations, maintenance, and security teams perform when they cannot spend days preparing for an inspection or exercise.“An effective nuclear deterrent must be ready 24/7/365,” said Maj. Gen. Colin Connor, commander of 20th Air Force. He described readiness as the force’s normal operating condition rather than something it builds up specifically for an exercise.Testing the force without a warningThe defining feature of Sentinel Dragon was its lack of traditional preparation time. Only a restricted group of planners knew the exercise was approaching. Operational units therefore had to rely on their normal command-and-control systems, respond to unexpected developments, and solve problems as they emerged.The assessment focused on three primary areas. Simulator evaluations of missile operators, maintenance activities conducted under pressure, and a complex scenario requiring security forces to recapture a launch facility.The operator evaluations used Missile Procedures Trainer simulations based on governing directives and technical requirements. The evaluation focused on first-tour crew members, who make up a significant part of the operational force.The objective was not simply to see whether personnel knew what to do, but whether they could execute required procedures precisely while operating under pressure. Maj. Jared Lynd, chief of the 20th Air Force Exercise Branch, said the ability to conduct a complex exercise involving multiple wings without advance notice was one of its most important results.Simulated drone attack tests launch-site securityThe launch-facility recapture scenario, added another layer to the exercise by bringing security and air units together in a simulated tactical environment.Security forces were required to manage complex airspace, respond to a simulated drone threat, and coordinate with the 582nd Helicopter Group for tactical insertion and air support. The scenario was intended to test the ability of different elements to operate as a single force rather than treating missile security as an isolated ground mission.At the same time, operations and maintenance personnel worked in the launch capsule and in the field to keep the weapon system secure and mission-capable during the simulated response.The exercise therefore combined nuclear-mission procedures with conventional security challenges, including an unmanned-aircraft threat and the need to regain control of a compromised launch facility.Lessons will shape future trainingSentinel Dragon was also designed to generate lessons for the Air Force’s future training program. The 20th Air Force said it will use observations from the exercise will be used to refine tactics and procedures. It also plans to standardize simulator scripts and training products across its missile wings.According to Air Force Global Strike Command, this could return hundreds of administrative man-hours to instructors by reducing the need for individual wings to develop and maintain similar training materials.That would let instructors spend more time on operational performance and warfighter training rather than administrative work. The exercise ultimately tested a simple but important premise for the US nuclear deterrent. Whether personnel responsible for operating, maintaining, and protecting the missile force can respond effectively when circumstances change without the luxury of a scheduled buildup period.The answer was that the personnel could integrate operations, maintenance, security, and air support under a scenario designed specifically to remove the advantage of advance preparation.

title: Probe over Tesla's Autopilot, Full-Self Driving systems? New concerns raised
content: A U.S. Congressman is demanding a probe over the safety and misuse of Tesla’s Autopilot and Full-Self Driving systems. Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL) has raised concerns as dozens of videos appearing to show Tesla driver asleep or otherwise disengaged behind the wheel while their vehicles were moving.Krishnamoorthi demanded that the Department of Transportation and National Highway Traffic Safety Administration take immediate action to address the misuse of Tesla’s Autopilot.Tesla’s Autopilot and Full Self-Driving require active driver supervisionIn a letter to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, Krishnamoorthi cited an NBC News investigation that identified 43 videos appearing to show individuals asleep in the driver’s seat of moving Teslas, including 17 posted this year alone. Tesla’s own documentation states that Autopilot and Full Self-Driving require active driver supervision and are not autonomous driving systems.“A recent NBC News investigation identified 43 videos that appear to show individuals asleep in the driver’s seat of moving Teslas, including 17 posted this year alone,” wrote Krishnamoorthi in the letter. “These incidents are particularly alarming because Autopilot and FSD require active driver supervision and are not autonomous driving systems. As these technologies become increasingly prevalent on American roads, DOT and NHTSA must ensure that manufacturers have adequate safeguards to prevent foreseeable misuse and that drivers are not encouraged to place dangerous levels of reliance on systems that still require their full attention.”Shortcomings identified in Tesla’s driver-engagement safeguardsKrishnamoorthi noted that NHTSA has previously identified shortcomings in Tesla’s driver-engagement safeguards. In an earlier engineering analysis of Autopilot, the agency concluded that Tesla’s system did not sufficiently ensure that drivers remained attentive and used the technology appropriately, identifying a mismatch between Autopilot’s substantial control over the vehicle and its safeguards for keeping drivers engaged.“Advising an alert driver who experiences a momentary lane drift to use a driver-assistance feature is one thing,” wrote Krishnamoorthi in the letter. “Encouraging a driver whom the vehicle has detected as drowsy to ‘stay focused with FSD’ presents a fundamentally different safety question. FSD requires continuous human supervision, yet the message appears to encourage use of the system precisely when the vehicle has detected that the driver may be less capable of providing that supervision.”The concerns come as NHTSA conducts an ongoing engineering analysis involving approximately 3.2 million Tesla vehicles equipped with FSD. The agency is examining whether FSD’s degradation-detection system can identify reduced roadway visibility and provide drivers with an adequate warning and sufficient time to respond. The investigation identifies nine incidents, including one fatality and one injury.Krishnamoorthi also raised concerns about messages Tesla reportedly began displaying to drivers with software update 2025.32.3. Those messages included “Drowsiness detected. Stay focused with FSD” and “Lane drift detected. Let FSD assist so you can stay focused.” Because FSD requires continuous human supervision, Krishnamoorthi questioned whether encouraging a driver whom the vehicle has already detected as drowsy to use the system creates an additional safety risk, according to a press release by the Congressman.

title: New hydrogen fuel cell produces 4 times more power with less platinum
content: A team of Chinese scientists has developed a novel proton-exchange membrane (PEM) fuel cell that delivers four times the power output of conventional designs. This advancement has the potential to enhance the practicality of hydrogen systems for vehicular and aerospace applications.This advancement addresses a significant challenge in hydrogen fuel cells, specifically the rate at which protons traverse the catalyst layer responsible for electricity generation. The researchers engineered a novel material interface that facilitates more efficient proton transport within the cell.Li Jie, an assistant professor at Beijing Institute of Technology (BIT) and a co-author of the study, said the new technology enables the “power stack of a fuel cell vehicle can be made smaller and lighter, and the vehicle can get stronger continuous output and a longer driving range.”A faster path for protonsPEM fuel cells typically operate at temperatures ranging from 140 to 176 degrees Fahrenheit and convert approximately 50 to 60 percent of hydrogen’s stored energy into electricity.Within the cell, hydrogen molecules release electrons and protons at the anode. Protons migrate across the electrolyte membrane, while electrons travel through an external circuit to generate electricity. At the cathode, protons and electrons combine with oxygen to produce water.The catalyst layer has long presented challenges. Materials such as Nafion can densely surround catalysts at the nanoscale, impeding the rapid transport of protons to reaction sites.The BIT team developed a Brønsted acid-Lewis base interface, providing additional sites for proton transfer. Experimental results demonstrated a tenfold increase in proton diffusion and a 6.5-fold improvement in proton conductivity. The activation energy was reduced by more than half.Four times more powerUnder standard operating conditions, the new fuel cell achieved 0.75 watts per square centimeter at 0.7 volts, representing approximately four times the power output of conventional designs.The system also demonstrated 6.9 kilowatts per gram of platinum, an important metric given the high cost of platinum as a fuel-cell catalyst. After 30,000 accelerated stress-test cycles, the new system retained 63 percent of its initial peak power, whereas conventional systems retained only 30 percent under identical conditions.The researchers indicated that the composite material can be produced at a practical scale. “In the lab right now, they can make about 100 grams in three days. That’s enough for 10 100-kilowatt-class stacks,” Li Jie stated.Possibility beyond road vehiclesThis technology may be advantageous in applications where weight, spatial constraints, and power density are critical considerations. The researchers emphasized its relevance for aerospace systems utilizing liquid oxygen, where efficient proton transport can significantly influence overall fuel-cell performance.“Our technology addresses how to generate power with higher efficiency and higher power density inside a smaller stack volume. This fits what aerospace energy systems need,” Li Jie said.This development coincides with the expansion of China’s hydrogen industry. By the end of 2025, the nation’s hydrogen production capacity exceeded 51 million tonnes per year. China also accounted for 53 percent of renewable-powered hydrogen projects utilizing electrolysis.Scaling remains the next testBy the end of 2025, China had approximately 32,000 fuel-cell vehicles in operation. In March 2026, three central government ministries set a target of 100,000 fuel-cell vehicles by 2030 and advocated for hydrogen prices to fall below 25 yuan, or about $3.50, per kilogram.The new technology must still demonstrate that it can be manufactured cost-effectively at an industrial scale while maintaining long-term safety and reliability.“Fuel cell vehicles don’t need to copy battery EVs. Battery EVs fit short trips. Fuel cells fit heavy trucks, long hauls, and cases that need quick refueling and long range,” Li Jie said.“Next, the team will build and test high-performance fuel cell stacks for different scenarios. We’ll also scale up the related materials and technology – and turn them into real-world products,” she added.The team published their findings in the journal Science.

title: New quantum sensor uses fibers thinner than hair, could replace GPS
content: Researchers at the Sandia National Laboratory (SNL) in the US have built a quantum sensor that uses just 5 milliwatts of power, about 2,000 times less than a standard LED bulb, and uses optical fibers that are just 420 nanometers thick, or 200 times thinner than human hair. The development of the sensor and associated technology paves the way for quantum sensing to be deployed in the field soon. The world relies heavily on satellite-based signals for navigation. From the app-based taxis to commercial aircraft, container ships at sea, and even military drones engaging in combat, all rely on satellite signals to know their position and navigate to their destinations. With such high dependence, it is easy to cripple systems by jamming or spoofing the satellite signals, and it can be done with a electromagnetic scream, which can drown out these signals. To overcome this, scientists have been working on quantum-based navigation systems which are not just unjammable but also highly accurate. There are different approaches to how such systems work, and one among them is free-space atom interferometry. In this approach, ultracold atoms are released in a vacuum chamber, and their motion is measured using lasers. However, vibrations or other disturbances can make these measurements unreliable, prompting scientists to look for a more contained approach. Tight lightA guided atom interferometry approach uses nonfibers to guide atoms in a tight light, much like marbles flowing through a narrow pipe. It ensures that they are constantly observed by the lasers. Jongmin Lee, a quantum sensing scientist at SNL, has been working to build an extremely small version of this device, one that consumes very little power and can be used in the field. Lee’s ambitious plan is to place this device on a photon-integrated circuit so measurements can continue even when the device is knocked around. In a real-world scenario, this could support navigation when a vehicle is moving through rough terrain or an aircraft is going through turbulence. “This idea has not been fully realized by the community for decades, due to challenges in dissipating heat from photonic devices in vacuum and in efficiently loading atoms around them,” explained Lee in a press release. Solving heat problemsLasers are needed to create a halo effect that can guide and count the moving atoms. Still, these are also major sources of heat in the system, especially when dealing with components like nanofibers that are much thinner than a human hair. In such situations, scientists have always had to make a trade-off. Either use a fragile design that loads atoms well but breaks under high heat conditions or a sturdy design that handles heat well but not the atoms. The SNL researchers led by Lee solved this problem by using small silicon pins that anchor the waveguide on either side and serve as heat sinks. “Building on our nanofiber results, we showed cesium atoms can be trapped with just five milliwatts of optical power and that atomic coherence can be measured using sub-microwatt fiber-coupled beams, all while minimizing in-vacuum heat loads,” added Lee in the press release. After resolving a few kinks in the setup, the team hopes to integrate the guide and other components on a chip and build a inertial quantum sensor array. The research findings were published in the journal AVS Quantum Science.

title: 390-MW nuclear reactor moves closer to approval with graphite report
content: Terrestrial Energy has submitted a Graphite Topical Report to the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), advancing the regulatory program for its Integral Molten Salt Reactor (IMSR) as the company works toward commercial deployment.The report seeks NRC approval of the company’s methodology for qualifying graphite used in the IMSR Core-unit, a central component of Terrestrial Energy’s Generation IV molten salt reactor design.The submission is the second of at least three IMSR Topical Reports the company expects to submit to the NRC in 2026. These reports are intended to address important technical and regulatory questions before Terrestrial Energy submits a future plant license application.Graphite is central to the IMSR designThe IMSR is a graphite-moderated molten salt reactor, meaning graphite is used as the reactor moderator while molten salt serves as the reactor’s fuel-bearing and heat-transfer medium.Although graphite has been used as a moderator in commercial nuclear reactors for decades, its behavior has to be demonstrated for each specific reactor design. Terrestrial Energy therefore has a dedicated qualification program to establish that its selected graphite can perform under the conditions expected inside the IMSR Core-unit.The company says it has spent several years collecting graphite performance data through testing at the NRG High Flux Reactor in Petten, Netherlands. The program has examined multiple nuclear graphite grades from multiple suppliers.Those results will support the qualification methodology described in the newly submitted report. According to Terrestrial Energy CEO Simon Irish, graphite performance ultimately determines the service life of the IMSR Core-unit. The company says the new submission begins the NRC review of the methodology it intends to use to qualify the material for commercial operation.Building the IMSR licensing basisThe Graphite Topical Report is part of a bigger pre-application engagement program between Terrestrial Energy and the NRC. The company previously received NRC approval for its Principal Design Criteria Topical Report in 2025 and its Postulated Initiating Events methodology Topical Report in 2026.Topical reports allow regulators to review specific technical and regulatory issues to be reviewed ahead of a full plant license application. Terrestrial Energy says approved reports can establish foundational elements of the IMSR licensing basis that may subsequently be referenced in future applications without requiring the same technical issues to be reevaluated.The company expects to submit at least three additional topical reports during 2026, addressing areas it considers consequential to the eventual licensing of an IMSR plant.The regulatory work is being carried out alongside engineering, testing, supply-chain development and commercial planning for Terrestrial Energy’s planned first commercial IMSR deployment in the early 2030s.A replaceable reactor coreThe graphite report also relates to an unusual aspect of Terrestrial Energy’s proposed commercial model. The IMSR Core-unit is designed to be replaceable.The company plans sequential Core-unit replacements on a roughly seven-year cycle during an IMSR plant’s operating life. Terrestrial Energy says this approach is central to its capital-light business model and could create recurring component-supply revenue after a plant is built. An IMSR plant can deliver 822 MWt of net thermal energy or 390 MWe of net electricity, or a customized combination of both.While the graphite qualification process remains an important regulatory step, the newly submitted report does not itself approve the IMSR for construction or operation. Rather, it asks the NRC to review the methodology Terrestrial Energy intends to use to demonstrate that its graphite can meet the requirements of the reactor’s intended operating conditions.

title: New Wildfire drone with over 9,200-mile-range unveiled for US military
content: General Atomics Aeronautical Systems Inc. (GA-ASI) has formally unveiled its new Wildfire unmanned aircraft, positioning the clean-sheet drone as a faster and more affordable successor to the MQ-9A Reaper. The company says Wildfire was designed to meet the Pentagon’s requirements for the emerging Massed Modular Aircraft (MMA) program while supporting long-endurance missions and future civil applications.According to GA-ASI, Wildfire can perform reconnaissance and strike missions traditionally handled by the Reaper. The company also sees potential uses outside combat, including commercial cargo transport, supported by its larger payload capacity and “stronger hardpoints.”“This is exactly the right design for high-demand missions and cost-conscious customers,” GA-ASI President David Alexander said in a press release. “Our tailor-designed, attrition-tolerant Wildfire balances the high capability our aircraft are known for with huge flexibility and great scalability. There’s never been anything like it before.”Built for the Pentagon’s new drone programThe Wildfire is being proposed for the Massed Modular Aircraft program, launched by the U.S. Air Force and Defense Innovation Unit in July. The initiative seeks a successor to the MQ-9 Reaper, with officials pushing for an aircraft that costs less and can be used in greater numbers.Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi, the Air Force’s chief modernization officer, recently said the program was accelerated after “concerning” Reaper losses during combat operations against Iran. The effort aims is field a more affordable and attritable unmanned aircraft.An MQ-9 can cost as much as $50 million depending on its configuration. Production of the aircraft ended last year, although the upgraded MQ-9B SkyGuardian remains in production.Wildfire targets longer range and heavier loadsThe Pentagon wants the MMA aircraft to cost roughly $10 million each, excluding mission equipment. Its solicitation calls for an aircraft capable of self-deploying 8,000 nautical miles (9,206 miles), while carrying at least 2,800 pounds of payload.The firm says Wildfire “meets or surpasses all requirements” in the solicitation. The company claims the aircraft can exceed 8,000 nautical miles of ferry range and carry two Long-Range Anti-Ship Missiles at the same time over meaningful combat distances.The aircraft can also accommodate different configurations of “munitions, launched effects, sensors or other payloads,” according to the company.Designed for faster productionThe Air Force initially set a fiscal 2031 target for the MMA program, with 20 mission-ready aircraft serving as the benchmark. GA-ASI says Wildfire could enter service years ahead of that schedule.The company also claims it can produce more than twice as many aircraft within the same timeframe. That approach reflects the Air Force’s growing focus on fielding more lower-cost unmanned systems.Wildfire is also designed for a highly autonomous operating model. GA-ASI says the aircraft will support collaborative operations from the beginning, allowing it to work alongside other systems.A modular approach to future upgradesThe MMA program is expected to follow a model similar to the Collaborative Combat Aircraft effort, which uses open architectures and successive design increments. GA-ASI and Anduril were recently selected for production deals under that program.Niemi has said the MMA aircraft is unlikely to rely on “cutting-edge ” technology. He expects the design to “probably” use a turboprop engine paired with “a long aspect wing.”GA-ASI’s Wildfire now enters a competition focused on cost, production speed, range, payload capacity, and adaptability as the Air Force seeks a new generation of attritable aircraft.

title: ProveKit: How on-device proofs could have stopped three of 2025's biggest ID leaks
content: On September 2, 2026, World open sourced ProveKit, a post quantum zero knowledge proving toolkit that lets a person prove a fact about themselves, such as being over 18 or holding a valid passport, without ever handing over the underlying document. The release, covered in detail by HackerNoon, landed the day after news broke of a dark web listing offering more than 170 million identity documents, including 153 million driver’s license scans, traced back to verification vendor IDScan.net.What ProveKit actually doesProveKit generates its proofs locally, on the user’s own phone or in the browser. Nothing is uploaded, nothing is copied to a server, and the verifying party receives only the answer to a single question, not the document itself. The toolkit has quietly powered World ID since April and now ships publicly under an MIT license after roughly two years of development and an independent audit by Least Authority.Under the hood, developers write circuits in Noir, the language built by Aztec for zero knowledge applications, which compile down to R1CS constraints and are proven using a Spartan based protocol with WHIR commitments. That combination targets 128 bit post quantum security and needs no trusted setup, unlike Groth16 or PLONK, which depend on a ceremony that has to be trusted forever. ProveKit is fast enough to complete a proof in seconds on a typical phone, and under thirty seconds on low end hardware, while working offline. It ships bindings for Swift, Kotlin, JavaScript and Rust, plus a C compatible interface, and developers can publish new provable claims without waiting on an app release cycle.Three Breaches This Could Have PreventedAU10TIX, 2024AU10TIX verifies identities for TikTok, Uber, X, Coinbase and PayPal. Exposed admin credentials sat active for over a year, giving anyone with the login a path into a logging platform holding names, birthdates, nationalities, ID numbers and links to scanned driver’s licenses and passports, as 404 Media reported. ProveKit’s model removes the central document store this attack depended on: the platform would only ever receive a proof of age or identity, never the image.Tea App, July 2025Tea, a women’s dating safety app, asked new users for a selfie and a government ID at signup. A legacy Firebase bucket was left open, and Security.org documented that roughly 13,000 selfies and ID photos leaked onto 4chan, despite Tea’s policy of deleting them after verification. A copycat app, TeaOnHer, suffered the same fate days later. A ProveKit style check needs no storage bucket at all, since there is nothing left to misconfigure once the document never leaves the phone.Discord, October 2025Discord’s age appeal process asked flagged users to send a selfie holding their government ID to a third party support vendor, 5CA. Attackers compromised a single support agent’s account and, according to Discord’s own statement, exposed roughly 70,000 government ID photos. A local proof of age would have let users clear the appeal without a document ever passing through a vendor’s support system.The PatternEach of these breaches began the same way: a document was collected to answer a yes or no question, then stored somewhere it eventually leaked. ProveKit’s bet is that the collection step was always the mistake. As Remco Bloemen of World stated, identity documents should only ever be authenticated with zero knowledge proofs. The tooling to do that on an ordinary phone has now shipped.

title: US Navy’s 268-pound torpedo targets China’s expanding submarine force
content: The US Navy is looking to make anti-submarine warfare less dependent on a small number of specialized aircraft by developing a compact torpedo delivery system that could be carried by carrier-based aircraft and unmanned platforms.The effort centers on the Silent Anvil Air-Launched Torpedo (SAA-LT), for which Naval Air Systems Command issued a request for information (RFI) to industry in August. Rather than simply replacing an existing torpedo, the program is aimed at expanding the number and types of aircraft that can participate in long-range submarine hunting.That distinction could become increasingly important in the western Pacific, where China is expanding its submarine force and where large aircraft such as the P-8A Poseidon could face increasingly contested operating environments.Why the Navy wants a smaller submarine-hunting weaponInteresting Engineering has explained the basic concept behind Silent Anvil, but the latest RFI reveals a broader operational objective. Putting a standoff anti-submarine weapon on more aircraft.The Navy wants SAA-LT to remain in the roughly 250-pound class, with a maximum weight of 268 pounds, a length of up to 70 inches and a diameter of 7.5 inches. Those dimensions are intended to make the weapon compatible with a much wider range of aircraft and unmanned platforms than larger air-launched systems.The RFI also calls for compatibility with the BRU-61/A weapons rack and both internal and external aircraft carriage. The system is also expected to work with carrier storage and handling equipment.The Navy is considering two approaches. A complete weapon integrating the glide vehicle and torpedo, or an unpowered wing kit capable of carrying a government-furnished anti-submarine weapon. The requirement calls for an end-to-end prototype demonstration within 18 months of an agreement, followed by approximately 180 prototype weapons over three years.China is changing the undersea equationUS naval intelligence estimates that China’s submarine force could reach roughly 80 boats by 2035, with about half potentially nuclear-powered. The projection represents a substantial change from China’s historically heavy reliance on conventionally powered submarines.China is also developing new submarine designs. Satellite imagery examined by the South China Morning Post (SCMP) in July showed a previously unidentified submarine at Shanghai’s Jiangnan Shipyard, with analysts suggesting its reduced sail and larger dimensions could indicate a new class. Its propulsion system remains unconfirmed.That larger and increasingly capable undersea force creates a problem for the US Navy: finding submarines is only part of the challenge. The aircraft that detect them must also be able to survive and operate across enormous distances in a contested Indo-Pacific battlespace.USNI News noted that the Navy’s interest in Silent Anvil comes alongside China’s expansion of its nuclear submarine fleet. It also highlighted the potential significance of bringing anti-submarine weapons back to carrier aviation, decades after the retirement of the S-3 Viking.Silent Anvil could spread the ASW missionThis is where the compact weapon could become more consequential than its size suggests. The US already has the High Altitude Anti-Submarine Warfare Weapon Capability (HAAWC), which combines a glide kit with the Mark 54 lightweight torpedo. HAAWC allows P-8A Poseidon aircraft to release the weapon from high altitude, but Silent Anvil is being designed to be considerably smaller.A smaller weapon potentially allows the Navy to distribute the attack function across more platforms instead of concentrating it on dedicated maritime patrol aircraft. That could include carrier-based aircraft and drones operating from locations where sending a large patrol aircraft would be difficult or risky.But that does not eliminate the hardest part of anti-submarine warfare which is finding the submarine in the first place. The RFI calls for Silent Anvil to have networked connectivity with tactical command-and-control systems, highlighting the importance of linking the weapon to a wider sensing and targeting network. The system therefore fits into a shift toward separating the platforms that detect a submarine from those that ultimately attack it.The network may be as important as the torpedoThat distributed approach also creates a new vulnerability. In a heavily contested Indo-Pacific environment, communications could be disrupted, aircraft could be forced farther from the search area, and the sensors responsible for finding submarines might not be operating from the same platform as the weapon.That makes connectivity between sensors, command networks, aircraft and weapons critical. The result is that Silent Anvil is less interesting as simply a smaller torpedo than as a potential building block for a more distributed US anti-submarine warfare architecture.The Navy’s immediate step is still only market research. Companies have until September 29 to respond to the RFI, with an industry day scheduled for September 17. Any resulting prototype program would still have to demonstrate that the concept works as an integrated system before production follows.If successful, however, Silent Anvil could give the US Navy something increasingly valuable in the western Pacific. More ways to put an anti-submarine weapon into the battlespace without relying entirely on a limited fleet of specialized submarine-hunting aircraft.

title: Hermeus gets FAA approval for Mach 1+ drone flights over New Mexico
content: Hermeus has secured approval from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to fly its Quarterhorse Mk 2.2 unmanned aircraft beyond Mach 1 during a limited test campaign over New Mexico.The authorization allows the U.S. aerospace company to conduct up to six supersonic flights over White Sands Missile Range by August 20, 2027. The operations must take place during daylight hours at or above 24,000 feet within restricted areas R-5111 A-D and R-5107.The approval comes as Hermeus develops Ramjet-X, an expendable ramjet-powered vehicle designed to be released from a reusable Quarterhorse aircraft. Although the authorization applies specifically to the Mk 2.2 test aircraft, it supports the company’s wider effort to expand access to high-speed flight testing.FAA clears Mach 1-plus testingHermeus petitioned the FAA on May 22, 2026, for permission to conduct developmental supersonic flights with the experimental Quarterhorse Mk 2.2. It later submitted several revisions, and the FAA received the final version on August 20.To meet its environmental obligations, the FAA adopted the U.S. Army’s categorical exclusion determination. That decision was based on the Army’s Record of Environmental Consideration for Quarterhorse operations at White Sands.The regulator determined that the proposed flights would not significantly affect the quality of the human environment. It also found that Hermeus’ request was within the intent of 14 CFR 91.818, the federal regulation governing civil supersonic flight testing.The permission is not open-ended. Hermeus can exceed Mach 1 only under the conditions and limitations specified in the special flight authorization.Reusable aircraft replaces expendable boosterRamjet engines require considerable forward speed before they can operate effectively. High-speed test vehicles have therefore traditionally relied on large, expensive boosters to reach the conditions needed for ramjet-powered flight.Hermeus plans to use Quarterhorse as a reusable launch platform instead. The aircraft will carry Ramjet-X to the required speed and altitude, then release it.Ramjet-X will then begin powered flight, while Quarterhorse returns for future missions.The approach is intended to remove the need for a purpose-built, expendable booster during every test. It could also make sustained high-Mach conditions more accessible for researchers and technology developers.Ramjet-X supports high-speed testing serviceHermeus plans to use Ramjet-X to offer high-Mach Flight Test as a Service. Customers will be able to test sensors, communications systems, autonomous technologies, computing equipment, materials, propulsion systems, and other experimental payloads under representative conditions.“High-speed flight testing is extremely expensive, and you don’t get many shots at it,” said Zach Shore, CEO of Hermeus. “Ramjet-X gives us a way to put new systems into sustained high-Mach environments without building an expensive one-off test program every time. Bringing speed, sustained flight, and scalability all into one system lowers the barriers to gathering extremely valuable data from these conditions and accelerates programs for both us and our customers,” he added.Hermeus is testing the Ramjet-X engine at its High Enthalpy Air-Breathing Test facility in Jacksonville, Florida. are company is developing high-temperature structures at its El Segundo, California, headquarters, with integrated vehicle testing planned for 2027.

title: New GPS-free positioning tech to be deployed in US military vehicles
content: The US Army will deploy an artificial intelligence-based positioning system that enables military vehicles to determine their location without relying on GPS or other radio-frequency signals. AI company TERN announced the deployment under an $11.26 million contract covering its Independently Derived Positioning System (IDPS) and Vehicle Health & Maintenance System (VHMS).The technology is intended to maintain navigation and fleet visibility when satellite signals are jammed, spoofed, degraded, or denied. Its rollout follows TERN’s progression through several Army innovation programs and moves the technology toward operational deployment.Vehicles determine their position without GPSTERN’s IDPS continuously derives and maintains a vehicle’s position independently of GPS and other external RF signals. It supplies positioning and navigation information to both the vehicle operator and associated command-and-control systems.This capability addresses a vulnerability that has become increasingly visible in modern conflicts. Operations in Ukraine and the Middle East have demonstrated how GPS and global navigation satellite system signals can be disrupted through interference, spoofing, denial, and electronic warfare.Such disruption can affect military maneuver, logistics, autonomous platforms, and coordination between commands. By calculating position within the vehicle, TERN’s system reduces dependence on signals travelling between satellites and ground-based platforms.“All of the space between a vehicle and the satellites orbiting Earth represents an opportunity to disrupt or degrade the GPS signal,” said Brett Harrison, president and co-founder of TERN. “TERN fundamentally changes that equation by enabling vehicles to derive their own position from within,” he added.“Rather than relying on an external signal, we are delivering the Army an intelligent positioning process that operates at the edge, fundamentally expanding what the vehicle is capable of doing,” Harrison continued. AI system combines location with vehicle healthAlongside navigation data, TERN’s VHMS continuously monitors vehicle condition and operational readiness. It combines that information with location data, giving commanders a unified view of fleet status within existing command environments.The combined capability could also support unmanned ground vehicles, robotic logistics systems, autonomous platforms, and other AI-enabled military operations. These machines need reliable positioning and readiness information as they assume greater responsibility for navigation, maneuver, and mission execution.TERN said continuously understanding both location and vehicle health provides a foundation for the intelligent systems operating above that layer.Army program moves technology into deploymentThe contract follows TERN’s earlier participation in the Army’s xTechOverWatch program. The company was selected from more than 600 applicants and secured a Direct-to-Phase II Small Business Innovation Research contract after an evaluation involving soldiers.Building on that work, TERN received a Phase III SBIR award through Army FUZE and the Technology Maturation Initiative. According to the company, the process moved its technology from Army innovation programs toward operational deployment in less than a year.“This award demonstrates what is possible when soldiers, acquisition leaders, and emerging technology companies have a clear path from operational experimentation to scaled fielding,” said Shaun Moore, CEO and co-founder of TERN.TERN said the same software-defined vehicle capabilities could also become relevant in commercial markets as autonomous systems continue to advance.

title: US firm to turn 250,000 tons of waste into power for data centers
content: Could the growing amount of waste be converted into energy? Recently, Kryonite Power has started talks with Los Angeles and San Diego to implement its waste-to-energy conversion systems.Every single day, the Golden State buries over 110,000 tons of garbage underground, which comes down to 40 million tons of material annually. Once buried, that trash festers into toxic methane and corrosive leachate, triggering environmental nightmares like the ongoing disaster at LA County’s Chiquita Canyon Landfill.A heat-releasing chemical reaction has been smoldering deep inside an inactive section of the Chiquita Canyon Landfill since early 2022. This underground reaction continues to break down buried waste at extreme temperatures. As a result, massive amounts of noxious gases escape from the site and drift into nearby neighborhoods. Surrounding residents face constant foul odors that have triggered thousands of official complaints to local regulators.Yet right beside this growing mountain of waste sits another massive issue: a tech-fueled hunger for electricity. Driven by artificial intelligence and expanding data centers, California’s energy demand is skyrocketing toward a projected 4,500 megawatts by 2040 (compared to 1,000 megawatts today). However, it turns out treating these two crises separately is a mistake. The company announced it has initiated early-stage talks with municipal leaders in Los Angeles and San Diego. Their proposal is straightforward: process raw urban waste and transform it into reliable, continuous electricity. “We believe California has been looking at two problems separately when they should be considered together,” said Lars Carlstrom, Founder of Kryonite Power. “Millions of tons of waste are being buried while California needs more reliable energy. We believe it is time to stop burying the problem and start turning it into a solution.”The need for power The offer lands right as California officials face a pressing dilemma. Conventional landfills are environmental disaster sites waiting to happen.These require decades of expensive monitoring, remediation, and community fallout management long after the last dump truck leaves. Meanwhile, tech giants and industrial operations are actively hunting for new power sources to run massive server farms. Intermittent renewables like solar and wind help, but cannot provide the uninterrupted baseload energy modern data infrastructure requires. Kryonite Power targets three primary operational areas for its technology. First, the company plans to intercept waste streams at active landfills before trash goes underground. Second, it aims to route municipal waste directly into specialized conversion plants during daily city collections. Finally, the system provides localized electricity generation to meet the heavy energy needs of data centers and industrial facilities.Waste-to-energy platformAs per its website, the firm provides a scalable infrastructure platform. Built on a standardized engineering design and procurement strategy, each unit scales easily to match local waste volumes, grid requirements, and regional market needs.For instance, the KPAX 250 belongs to a regional design class that can process 250,000 tons of waste per year. Built to serve entire counties or metropolitan clusters, this facility delivers a generation capacity of 20–30 MW in continuous electrical output. It provides a scalable energy solution for mid-to-large urban regions through the conversion of large municipal waste streams into steady power.It is an ambitious pitch. Waste-to-energy technologies typically face political, environmental, and financial hurdles before getting off the ground.Still, with cities running out of landfill space and power grids straining under the weight of the digital revolution, local officials may be more willing than ever to test whether California’s garbage can power its technological future.

title: US opens first rare earth recycling plant, can process 27,500 tons
content: A new facility in Arizona is turning discarded products into a domestic source of rare earth materials at a commercial scale. Cyclic Materials, a company that recycles rare earth magnets from end-of-life products, has opened the plant in Mesa. It can process up to 25,000 metric tons (27,500 U.S. tons) of magnet-bearing material every year using automated mechanical separation technology. Commercial operations are already underway. The facility will supply recovered rare earth magnet material and other critical metals to U.S. customers, with its first commercial shipments expected later this month.Automated magnet separation at commercial scaleThe Mesa plant represents the first commercial-scale deployment of Cyclic Materials’ proprietary MagCycle technology.  The system automatically separates magnets from discarded products before the recovered materials move through the company’s wider rare earth processing platform.This recovered material includes Mag-Xtract, Cyclic Materials’ rare earth magnet product. The plant can also reclaim copper, aluminum and steel, allowing several valuable materials inside old equipment to return to manufacturing supply chains.Automating this initial separation stage could help process large and varied streams of magnet-bearing waste. Such magnets are found across products used in the automotive, robotics, electronics, energy, defense and artificial intelligence industries.Cyclic Materials has already received more than 7,000 metric tons (7,700 U.S. tons) of feedstock at the Mesa site. It has also secured further volumes through long-term commercial partnerships established across the United States.Turning old products into domestic resourcesRare earth elements are essential to many modern technologies, including electric motors, electronics, and advanced defense systems. However, their global supply chain remains concentrated in a few regions, making manufacturers vulnerable to trade disruptions and geopolitical tensions.Recovering the materials from end-of-life products offers another route to supply. Instead of allowing magnet-bearing devices to enter conventional waste streams, recycling facilities can extract their valuable components and feed them back into domestic production.The approach does not eliminate the need for newly mined materials. However, it can help the United States recover resources already extracted, processed, and incorporated into manufactured products.The timing is also significant. Global demand for rare earth elements is projected to triple by 2035 as industries expand their use of electric vehicles, robotics, AI infrastructure, electronics, and clean-energy systems.Facility completed in 17 monthsCyclic Materials completed the Mesa facility 17 months after first announcing the project. According to the company, the relatively short construction period demonstrates a model that could be repeated to establish additional domestic processing capacity.The site acts as the front end of the company’s integrated rare earth recovery platform. Magnets removed through the MagCycle process can be directed toward further processing, while recovered copper, aluminum and steel can also re-enter manufacturing streams.Its opening gives Cyclic Materials its first commercial-scale operating base for automated magnet recovery in the United States. With thousands of tons of feedstock already delivered and customer shipments approaching, the plant is moving beyond a pilot operation into commercial production.The company says the facility is the first commercial-scale automated rare earth magnet recovery plant of its kind in the country.

title: Analog memory chip achieves 100 times greater precision
content: Future electronics could be more energy-efficient than today’s. Researchers at Sandia National Laboratories have unveiled a new computer memory technology that breaks away from standard binary computing. The new technology is dubbed ETCRAM, which is short for electro-thermo-chemical random-access memory. It could help cut energy use across the tech industry. ETCRAM uses localized heating and electrical pulses within tantalum and vanadium oxide materials to store a continuous range of analog values. “ETCRAM is able to achieve 100 times higher precision than existing state-of-the-art technology — and at least three orders of magnitude greater dynamic range. That’s the value of a number that you can store in analog,” said Elliot Fuller, Sandia researcher. Electrothermochemical random access memory chips are able to achieve 100 times higher precision than existing state-of-the-art technology. (Photo by Arianna Andreatta)Moving beyond 1s and 0sSince the dawn of the digital age, silicon chips have processed information strictly as ones and zeros. Turn the switch on, you get a one. Flip it off, you get a zero. While this binary framework was built for the modern world, it wastes massive amounts of power by forcing complex calculations through two-state pipelines.ETCRAM throws out those constraints. Rather than choosing between on or off, the new memory technology stores a continuous range of analog values. The team says it is like a rechargeable battery“You can think of ETCRAM as a memory device. You can charge a battery halfway and then stop charging and use that energy. Think of the state of the battery as a memory. It stores that state,” researcher Alec Talin explained. ETCRAM works similarly, using localized heat and electrical pulses to trap distinct physical states inside materials like tantalum and vanadium oxide. “The technology that we’ve developed is designed to overcome a limitation of our existing computing technology to really improve energy efficiency,” added Fuller. The performance gains were huge. Fuller notes that ETCRAM delivers 100 times higher precision and at least three orders of magnitude greater dynamic range than existing analog memory devices. The key was a physics trick: self-heating. Electrochemistry is typically slow. But by triggering micro-bursts of heat right as the electrical pulse hits, the device speeds up, locking in precise analog values without pulling massive amounts of power. Smart sensors, lower powerThe energy reduction could not come at a better time. With artificial intelligence expanding rapidly, data centers are consuming power at alarming rates.Federal estimates project that server electricity consumption in the US could skyrocket to roughly 800 billion kilowatt-hours annually by 2050. Replacing power-hungry silicon memory with analog components like ETCRAM could bend that demand curve downward.This development is especially important for edge computing, as it lets hardware like camera sensors perform complex data analysis directly on the device, reducing both energy use and data-transmission delays.In edge computing, the data is processed right where it is collected instead of sending it back to distant cloud servers. Imagine a smart security camera analyzing video in real time on its own internal sensor, or an autonomous vehicle making split-second decisions without lag.With this development, the future of computing might be analog, self-heating, and surprisingly efficient.

title: Honda backs US-made magnets to cut rare-earth supply dependence
content: Honda Motor has invested in Niron Magnetics, a US company commercializing rare-earth-free Iron Nitride permanent magnets. Announced on September 9, the investment will support the continued commercialization of Niron’s technology and help scale its manufacturing operations.The move reflects Honda’s interest in next-generation magnetic materials that could reduce reliance on rare-earth elements in electrified systems.Reducing reliance on rare-earth materialsPermanent magnets are used in electric propulsion motors and several other technologies. However, many conventional high-performance magnets depend on rare-earth metals that face resource constraints and changing market conditions.Niron’s Iron Nitride technology offers an alternative that does not require rare-earth materials. It is intended to support performance, cost stability, and sustainability goals while reducing reliance on constrained global supply chains.“This investment reflects the increasing focus on rare-earth-free magnet technology as manufacturers look for more resilient solutions,” said Jonathan Rowntree, CEO of Niron Magnetics. “Following investment from Honda, we are encouraged by their confidence in our technology and vision for scaling rare-earth-free permanent magnets across a broad range of applications. The investment adds to growing industry momentum as manufacturers increasingly direct resources to alternatives to rare-earth-based magnets,” he added.The technology can be used across automotive systems, robotics, industrial automation and emerging mobility platforms. Other potential applications include artificial intelligence and data center infrastructure, as well as consumer electronics.Honda sees potential for electric propulsionMost electric propulsion motors currently use permanent magnets made from rare-earth metals. Honda expects Niron’s technology to help address some of the supply and market challenges associated with these materials.“Niron Magnetics has an innovative permanent magnet technology that does not require rare earth materials. Most electric propulsion motors today use permanent magnets made from rare earth metals, which are subject to resource constraints and fluctuations in market conditions,” said Mahito Shikama, Director, Executive Officer of Honda Motor Co., Ltd.“Niron Magnetics is addressing these challenges, and Honda has high hopes for its potential,” he added. The investment further supports Niron’s effort to establish Iron Nitride as a new category of permanent magnetic material. It will also help the company expand the technology’s adoption across a growing range of products and applications.Honda’s backing adds to the resources being directed toward alternatives to rare-earth-based permanent magnets. For Niron, it supports the transition from commercializing its technology to producing the magnets at a larger scale.US facility to scale magnet productionNiron recently announced a new 287,000-square-foot facility in Sartell, Minnesota, for magnet manufacturing. The plant is scheduled to begin operating in 2027.Once operational, the facility is expected to produce up to 1,500 tons of rare-earth-free Iron Nitride permanent magnets annually. This output will serve the company’s targeted automotive, industrial and advanced technology applications.The facility forms a central part of Niron’s manufacturing expansion. Honda’s investment will support the company as it works to scale production and broaden the use of Iron Nitride magnets across electrified systems.

title: Flying stratospheric platform completes 18,000-mile trip, returns to US
content: A Moriarty-based company’s stratospheric platform has re-entered the United States. High Altitude Platform Systems (HAPS) for stratospheric infrastructure completed its record-breaking trans-Pacific flight from New Mexico to Japan and back. Callled Service Test 1 (ST1) mission, the stratospheric platform was developed by Sceye. ST1 launched on August 9, 2026, and arrived in Japan 13 days later. While operating in Japan, Sceye demonstrated mobile broadband connectivity to unmodified devices through SoftBank Corp.’s core network and HAPS-based edge computing and communication with drones to support the development of a 3D communications network.Mission validated technology, vehicle systems, payload“Groundbreaking and historic only begin to describe our ST1 flight,” says Mikkel Vestergaard Frandsen, Founder and CEO of Sceye. “This mission proved not only that our technology, vehicle systems, payload, and operational infrastructure are ready for connectivity services, but also that the stratosphere is where the future non-terrestrial infrastructure lies. The stratosphere is what will enable the always-on future – including the promised land of 6G. Together ground, stratosphere, and space – each operating at their optimal strengths, will change the course of humanity.”During its journey, Sceye’s ST1 traveled nearly 30,000 km and re-entered continental U.S. on September 4, 2026. ST1 reached airspace near Sceye’s headquarters in Moriarty, New Mexico on September 5, 2026, where Sceye completed additional vehicle testing and a planned termination and descent.Conducted in partnership with SoftBank Corp, a leading operator of telecommunications and IT businesses in Japan and globally, ST1 marks Sceye’s first flight to Asia and a groundbreaking milestone toward the commercial deployment of HAPS as stratospheric infrastructure. ST1 carried SceyeCELL, a first-of-its-kind “cell tower in the sky” designed to deliver wide-area mobile broadband directly to standard devices from the stratosphere. When deployed at full scale, one Sceye HAPS is designed to cover the equivalent area of approximately 500 terrestrial towers, according to a press release.Stratosphere offers the optimal vantage pointThe stratosphere offers the optimal vantage point: It is close enough to Earth for high-capacity connectivity and observation, yet the altitude is high enough for wide-area reach. Importantly, the stratosphere offers space-like conditions without the cost of being in space and the disadvantages of being in orbit. Sceye’s HAPS maintain altitude and their area of operation in the stratosphere through consecutive day and night cycles, operating like geostationary satellites, only 1,800 times closer to Earth and at a fraction of the cost, as per the release. The platform traveled nearly 30,000 km from New Mexico to Japan and back to New Mexico over a month-long journey. The platform also tested emergency calls, using an emergency alert messaging system designed for large-scale disasters, as well as communications with drones.Through a server installed on the HAPS, Sceye and SoftBank conducted data processing directly on the platform, demonstrating an average round-trip processing response time of 68 milliseconds, reducing communications latency by over 40% compared with internet-based cloud processing. This marks the world’s first successful test in which a mobile core network and a web server for processing were installed on a HAPS, enabling response processing to be performed entirely onboard the HAPS and the results to be relayed back to smartphones.

title: Multi-kilojoule fusion lasers could power next-gen US air defense
content: RTX Ventures has invested in laser fusion company Xcimer Energy to develop pulsed-laser technology for potential use in US military directed-energy systems.The collaboration brings together two applications that share a fundamental engineering challenge: building powerful lasers that can fire repeatedly, reliably and affordably.Xcimer is developing excimer laser technology for its fusion power system. The company says the same approach could provide the performance and scalability needed for directed-energy weapons, potentially offering longer-range capability than existing systems.RTX’s investment is also intended to support Xcimer’s fusion program. In June, the US Department of Energy approved Xcimer’s fusion pilot power plant design under its Milestone-Based Fusion Development Program.One laser, two missionsLaser fusion works by using intense laser pulses to compress and heat fuel until it reaches conditions where nuclear fusion can occur. The challenge is developing lasers that can deliver these pulses repeatedly while keeping energy consumption, maintenance, and operating costs under control.Those same requirements matter for military laser systems. A directed-energy weapon must deliver enough energy to engage a target while remaining efficient and reliable enough for repeated use. Xcimer says its excimer-based system is designed around those requirements.“As the United States accelerates the development of next-generation air defense, the need for affordable and scalable directed energy systems has never been more urgent,” said Conner Galloway, co-founder, CEO and Chief Science Officer at Xcimer. “Our excimer-based laser technology offers the performance, speed and inherent scalability needed at a fraction of the cost and complexity of today’s systems.”The partnership will now examine how the laser technology could be integrated and containerized into RTX defense systems.That could be important because one of the challenges facing directed-energy weapons is making them practical outside laboratory environments. Systems must fit into deployable platforms while generating enough power to engage threats.Fusion technology enters air defenseRTX brings experience in sensing, command and control, and air-defense systems to the partnership. The company says those capabilities could help integrate Xcimer’s laser technology into future defense platforms.“We believe Xcimer’s pulsed-laser technology lines up perfectly with our expertise in areas like advanced sensing, command and control and air defense,” said RTX Chief Technology Officer Juan de Bedout. “Together we will explore how we can best integrate these technologies into advanced, scalable defense systems able to defeat a range of new and evolving threats.”Xcimer is pursuing commercial fusion power alongside the defense work. The company expects its fusion technology to begin delivering electricity to the grid by the mid-2030s.The dual-use development could give the laser technology two potential markets: commercial fusion energy and military directed-energy systems.For now, the RTX-Xcimer agreement is focused on exploring integration and development rather than announcing an operational weapon. The companies will need to demonstrate that the laser can meet the demanding requirements of a deployable defense system while maintaining the efficiency, reliability, and scalability needed for repeated operation.
